title: [Bug]: Reservation reseed marks actual cost applied without incrementing it
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I searched open and closed issues before filing
- [x] [#28283](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/28283) concerns unrelated spend-counter inflation and does not cover this reseed branch

### What happened?

When a reserved spend counter disappears, becomes non-numeric, or is reset below the value needed for reconciliation, `_set_reserved_entry_actual_cost` decides that the reservation adjustment cannot be applied

With `reseed_on_inconsistent=True`, it calls `reseed_spend_counter_from_db`. That database value is explicitly documented as a lagging floor because entity spend is flushed asynchronously and can exclude the current request

After reseeding, the function does not increment the counter by the current request's actual cost or reapply the reservation delta. It still sets `entry["applied_adjustment"]` to the target value as though reconciliation succeeded

The caller returns the entry's counter key in `reserved_counter_keys`, so the direct increment path skips that key. The current request's actual cost can therefore be absent from live budget enforcement until a later durable flush and reseed

### Steps to Reproduce

This focused harness forces the inconsistent-counter branch

```python
import asyncio
from unittest.mock import AsyncMock, patch

import litellm.proxy.proxy_server as ps
import litellm.proxy.spend_tracking.budget_reservation as br

async def main():
    entry = {
        "counter_key": "spend:key:demo",
        "reserved_cost": 0.4,
        "applied_adjustment": 0.0,
    }
    increment = AsyncMock()
    reseed = AsyncMock()

    with (
        patch.object(br, "_counter_can_apply_adjustment", AsyncMock(return_value=False)),
        patch.object(ps, "_increment_spend_counter_cache", increment),
        patch.object(ps, "reseed_spend_counter_from_db", reseed),
    ):
        await br._set_reserved_entry_actual_cost(
            entry=entry,
            actual_cost=0.7,
            default_reserved_cost=0.4,
        )

    print({
        "reseed_calls": reseed.await_count,
        "increment_calls": increment.await_count,
        "applied_adjustment": entry["applied_adjustment"],
    })

asyncio.run(main())
```

Current output is equivalent to

```text
{'reseed_calls': 1, 'increment_calls': 0, 'applied_adjustment': 0.3}
```

The function records that the 0.3 adjustment was applied even though no increment occurred. Because the durable entity update is queued before counter reconciliation, the reseed can still read the pre-request database floor

### Expected behavior

After a reseed, apply the current actual cost in a way that cannot clobber concurrent increments, or signal the caller that this key was not reconciled so the full direct increment runs

Regression coverage should exercise actual cost greater than, equal to, and less than the reservation with missing, reset, and non-numeric counters

### Relevant code

- [Inconsistent-counter reseed and unconditional applied marker](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/spend_tracking/budget_reservation.py#L741-L789)
- [Lagging-floor documentation](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py#L2240-L2295)
- [Reserved keys skipped by direct increment](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py#L2350-L2445)
- [Database update precedes counter reconciliation](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/hooks/proxy_track_cost_callback.py#L476-L534)

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

### What LiteLLM version are you on?

v1.96.0, commit `b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8`

title: [Bug]: Failed reservation cleanup can double-count actual spend
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I searched open and closed issues before filing
- [x] I found no issue covering the combined reconcile-failure and counter-invalidation-failure path

### What happened?

When post-call budget reservation reconciliation raises, `_reconcile_budget_reservation_for_counter_update` attempts to invalidate all reserved counters and then returns an empty reserved-key set so the caller applies the full actual cost directly

That fallback is correct only if invalidation succeeded for every reserved key. If invalidation also raises, the function still returns an empty set. Any counter that retained its original reservation is then incremented by the full actual cost, leaving `previous_spend + reserved_cost + actual_cost`

The invalidation helper processes keys sequentially, so this can also leave a mixed state where some scopes were deleted and others retained their reservation. Treating all keys as unreserved cannot reconcile that partial result safely

The consequence is conservative over-counting rather than lost billing, but it can produce false budget exhaustion and persistent 429 responses until a durable reseed repairs the affected counter

### Steps to Reproduce

This focused harness reproduces the control-flow invariant without a provider or database

```python
import asyncio
from unittest.mock import AsyncMock, MagicMock, patch

import litellm.proxy.proxy_server as ps
import litellm.proxy.spend_tracking.budget_reservation as br

async def main():
    reservation = {"entries": [{"counter_key": "spend:key:demo"}]}
    with (
        patch.object(br, "get_reserved_counter_keys", MagicMock(return_value={"spend:key:demo"})),
        patch.object(br, "reconcile_budget_reservation", AsyncMock(side_effect=RuntimeError("reconcile failed"))),
        patch.object(br, "invalidate_budget_reservation_counters", AsyncMock(side_effect=RuntimeError("delete failed"))),
    ):
        result = await ps._reconcile_budget_reservation_for_counter_update(reservation, 0.7)

    print(result)

asyncio.run(main())
```

Current output is `set()`, which tells `increment_spend_counters` to run the full direct increment even though cleanup did not establish that the reservation was removed

A full regression test should start from a counter containing a known reservation, fail reconciliation and deletion for that key, run `increment_spend_counters`, and assert the final value contains actual cost exactly once

### Expected behavior

Track cleanup success per counter and choose a deterministic recovery for each key

Possible safe approaches include returning retained keys so direct increment skips them, reseeding retained keys from durable spend plus the current actual cost, or making cleanup and fallback application an atomic script

### Relevant code

- [Reconcile fallback always returns an empty set](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py#L2534-L2566)
- [Direct increment skips only returned reserved keys](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py#L2350-L2445)

title: [Bug]: Recovered partial stream cost is released from live budget counters
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I searched open and closed issues before filing
- [x] [#14457](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/14457) covers missing usage recovery for terminated streams, not budget-counter reconciliation after cost has been recovered

### What happened?

The failure hook now recovers partial usage and cost from a stream that failed after delivering chunks, but the budget reservation is finalized as zero before that recovered cost is processed

`async_post_call_failure_hook` first calls `release_budget_reservation`, which reconciles every reserved counter to `actual_cost=0`. Later in the same hook, a valid `combined_usage_object` causes `recovered_response_cost` to be passed to `update_database`

The database writer does more than the original failure report suggested. It writes a failure spend log and schedules durable key, user, team, organization, end-user, and related entity updates. The missing part is the live enforcement path: the failure hook never calls `increment_spend_counters` or reconciles the reservation to `recovered_response_cost`

Until the asynchronous database updates flush and a later counter repair observes them, the shared budget counters omit cost that LiteLLM already calculated and recorded

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure a priced streaming model and a key with a low `max_budget`
2. Start a stream and allow several billed chunks to arrive
3. Force a mid-stream provider read error so `combined_usage_object` and `response_cost` are available
4. Observe that the failure spend-log payload records the recovered positive cost
5. Inspect the corresponding live `spend:key:*` counter and observe that the pre-call reservation was refunded instead of reconciled to that cost

Current unit coverage demonstrates the split behavior

```shell
pytest -q   tests/test_litellm/proxy/hooks/test_proxy_track_cost_callback.py::test_async_post_call_failure_hook_releases_budget_reservation_before_route_skip   tests/test_litellm/proxy/hooks/test_proxy_track_cost_callback.py::test_async_post_call_failure_hook_records_recovered_partial_spend
```

Both tests pass: one establishes unconditional release at hook entry and the other establishes the later positive database cost. There is no assertion that the live spend counter receives that cost

### Expected behavior

When recovered partial cost is positive, reconcile the existing reservation to that actual cost through the same counter path used by successful requests

Only release to zero when no billed usage or cost can be recovered

### Relevant code

- [Failure hook release and recovered-cost write](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/hooks/proxy_track_cost_callback.py#L48-L178)
- [Success path updates database and counters](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/hooks/proxy_track_cost_callback.py#L476-L534)
- [Release reconciles to zero](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/spend_tracking/budget_reservation.py#L272-L276)

title: [Bug]: Global proxy spend cache loses concurrent increments
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I searched open and closed issues before filing
- [x] [#34732](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/34732) covers the separate `max_budget_per_session` admission race

### What happened?

The cache used to enforce `litellm.max_budget` is updated with a non-atomic read, add, and set sequence

After each successful request, `update_cache` reads `GLOBAL_PROXY_SPEND_CACHE_KEY`, computes `global_proxy_spend + response_cost`, and schedules an asynchronous `async_set_cache_pipeline`. Two concurrent callbacks can both read the same starting value and both write their own result, permanently losing one increment from the cached global spend

The auth path reads this cached scalar through the event-driven coordinator and passes it to `_global_proxy_budget_check`. Under sustained concurrency, a lost-update value can be kept alive by later writes that refresh the cache TTL, so this is more than the ordinary delay before a completed request becomes visible

There is also no pre-call reservation for the global proxy budget. Even if the post-call update were atomic, concurrent requests can all be admitted against the same below-budget value. The existing key, team, user, organization, end-user, and tag reservation flow does not include the proxy-global counter

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Set `litellm.max_budget` slightly above the current global spend
2. Warm `GLOBAL_PROXY_SPEND_CACHE_KEY` with value `10.0`
3. Complete two requests concurrently with `response_cost=1.0`
4. Arrange for both `update_cache` calls to read before either scheduled pipeline write runs
5. Observe two writes of `11.0` instead of a final value of `12.0`
6. Send concurrent requests near the budget and observe that all can pass the same pre-call check before their costs are recorded

A deterministic regression test can use a cache double with a barrier in `async_get_cache`, capture the two pipeline payloads, and assert the final global scalar is the sum of both costs

### Expected behavior

Use an atomic shared increment for completed global spend and include the global budget in the pre-call reservation or atomic compare-and-reserve flow

The completed-spend counter should also be reconciled from the durable proxy budget row without allowing fire-and-forget cache writes to extend a stale value indefinitely

### Relevant code

- [Global spend load during auth](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/auth/user_api_key_auth.py#L1976-L1992)
- [Global budget comparison](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py#L356-L371)
- [Non-atomic cache update](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py#L2909-L2916)
- [Fire-and-forget shared set](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py#L3076-L3094)

title: [Bug]: Project updates leave blocked, model, and budget auth state stale
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I searched open and closed issues before filing
- [x] [#25553](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/25553) is related cache-coherence work for virtual keys but does not cover project objects or `/project/update`

### What happened?

The enterprise `POST /project/update` endpoint updates the project row and its budget or object-permission rows, then returns without refreshing or invalidating `project_id:{project_id}`

Authentication resolves projects through that cache key first. `_run_project_checks` then trusts the cached `blocked`, `models`, and budget values. A warmed project can therefore continue using its previous authorization state after an admin blocks it, restricts its models, or lowers its budget

The stale direction also affects availability. Unblocking a project or widening its model access can continue to reject requests until the management-object cache expires

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create an enterprise project with `blocked=False` and attach a key
2. Send one LLM request to warm `project_id:{project_id}`
3. Call `POST /project/update` with `blocked=True`
4. Confirm the database row is blocked
5. Send another request before the management-object cache expires
6. Observe that `get_project_object` returns the cached unblocked project and the request is admitted

The same sequence can be repeated by replacing `blocked` with a restrictive `models` update or a lower budget

### Expected behavior

After every successful project mutation, update or invalidate `project_id:{project_id}` and any cached included budget or permission data before returning

Regression coverage should warm the project cache, mutate blocked, models, and budget independently, and assert that the next auth check observes each change

### Relevant code

- [Project update returns after the DB write](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/enterprise/litellm_enterprise/proxy/management_endpoints/project_endpoints.py#L650-L681)

title: [Bug]: Team block and unblock leave cached auth state unchanged
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I searched open and closed issues before filing
- [x] I found no issue covering cache invalidation in `/team/block` or `/team/unblock`

### What happened?

`POST /team/block` says it blocks all calls from keys with the team ID, but both the block and unblock endpoints only update Postgres

Authentication resolves teams through cache key `team_id:{team_id}` before reading the database, and `common_checks` enforces `team_object.blocked` from that cached object. If traffic has already cached `blocked=False`, calls continue after the database row is blocked until the cache expires. The inverse stale state rejects traffic after an unblock

This is inconsistent with other team mutations. The module already defines `_refresh_cached_team` and its docstring says every endpoint that mutates `litellm_teamtable` must call it so auth does not keep granting revoked permissions. The block and unblock endpoints omit that call

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create an unblocked team and a key assigned to it
2. Send one LLM request to warm `team_id:{team_id}`
3. Call `POST /team/block` for the team
4. Confirm the database row has `blocked=True`
5. Send another request before the management-object cache TTL expires
6. Observe that auth uses the cached `blocked=False` team and admits the request
7. Let the cache refresh and call `/team/unblock`
8. Observe the inverse stale rejection until another refresh

In a multi-pod deployment, each pod can retain its own warmed management-object cache, extending the inconsistent window across replicas

### Expected behavior

After a successful block or unblock update, refresh or invalidate `team_id:{team_id}` through `_refresh_cached_team` before returning

Regression coverage should warm the cache, execute each endpoint, and assert that the very next auth check sees the new blocked state

### Relevant code

- [Block and unblock endpoints](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/team_endpoints.py#L4092-L4184)
- [Existing cache refresh helper](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/team_endpoints.py#L291-L319)

title: [Bug]: Customer block and unblock APIs do not consistently enforce EndUser.blocked
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I searched open and closed issues before filing
- [x] Existing end-user budget reports such as [#34238](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/34238) concern spend counters, not the `blocked` field

### What happened?

`POST /customer/block` documents that subsequent LLM requests carrying the blocked end-user ID will be rejected, but the core auth path never checks `LiteLLM_EndUserTable.blocked`

The endpoint writes `blocked=True` to Postgres even when the optional enterprise blocked-user callback is not configured. `get_end_user_object` loads that row for budget checks, but `common_checks` only checks the end-user budget and does not reject a blocked object. In an OSS or enterprise deployment without that callback, the block API succeeds while later requests continue

The optional enterprise callback does check the database field, but it caches the result under `litellm:end_user_id:{id}` for 60 seconds. `/customer/block` does not invalidate that cache or the core auth cache `end_user_id:{id}`, so a warmed unblocked entry remains usable until expiry

The inverse endpoint has a separate consistency problem. `POST /customer/unblock` requires the enterprise callback and removes the ID from `litellm.blocked_user_list`, but it never updates `LiteLLM_EndUserTable.blocked` back to `False`. A user blocked through `/customer/block` can therefore remain blocked by the callback after its cache refresh even though `/customer/unblock` returned success

### Steps to Reproduce

Core enforcement gap

1. Run the proxy with Postgres and without the enterprise blocked-user callback
2. Call `POST /customer/block` with `{"user_ids":["blocked-demo"]}`
3. Confirm the database row has `blocked=True`
4. Send an LLM request with `"user":"blocked-demo"`
5. Observe that core auth admits the request

Enterprise cache gap

1. Configure the enterprise blocked-user callback and make one request as `cached-demo` to cache `blocked=False`
2. Call `POST /customer/block` for that ID
3. Send another request within 60 seconds
4. Observe that the callback reads the stale unblocked cache entry

Unblock persistence gap

1. Block an ID through `/customer/block`
2. Call `/customer/unblock`
3. Inspect `LiteLLM_EndUserTable.blocked` and observe it is still `True`
4. Let the enterprise cache expire and retry the request
5. Observe that the persisted row can block the user again

### Expected behavior

`/customer/block` and `/customer/unblock` should update the same durable field, invalidate both cache namespaces, and core auth should enforce the durable `blocked` state without requiring an optional callback

### Relevant code

- [Block endpoint and documented contract](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/customer_endpoints.py#L55-L105)
- [Unblock endpoint](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/customer_endpoints.py#L108-L168)

title: [Bug]: Reused x-litellm-call-id silently drops spend-log rows
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I searched open and closed issues before filing
- [x] [#28562](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/28562) is related to passthrough call ID correlation but does not cover primary-key collisions or dropped rows

### What happened?

The proxy accepts a caller-provided `x-litellm-call-id` and uses it as the fallback `LiteLLM_SpendLogs.request_id` whenever the response has no provider ID, including failure and passthrough-style logging paths

`LiteLLM_SpendLogs.request_id` is the table primary key. Spend-log batches are inserted with `create_many(..., skip_duplicates=True)`, so a repeated call ID does not produce an error or a second row. It is silently skipped

A client can therefore reuse one header value across many requests and retain only the first per-request spend-log row. Aggregate key, user, and team spend updates use separate queues, so this does not directly bypass aggregate accounting, but it does make the request audit trail, per-request cost lookup, and analytics incomplete

The trace identifier and durable spend-log identifier currently have incompatible trust and uniqueness requirements. The trace ID is intentionally client-controlled, while the spend-log primary key must be server-generated and unique

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Send two requests that reach a logging path without a provider response ID, using the same `x-litellm-call-id: repeated-id`
2. Wait for the spend-log queue to flush
3. Query `/spend/logs?request_id=repeated-id`
4. Observe that only one row exists even though both requests reached spend tracking

The ID selection itself can be reproduced without a provider call

```python
from litellm.proxy.spend_tracking.spend_tracking_utils import get_spend_logs_id

kwargs = {"litellm_call_id": "repeated-id"}

assert get_spend_logs_id("pass_through_endpoint", {}, kwargs) == "repeated-id"
assert get_spend_logs_id("pass_through_endpoint", {}, kwargs) == "repeated-id"
```

The later insert uses `skip_duplicates=True`, so the second row is discarded as an expected duplicate

### Expected behavior

Every request that reaches spend tracking receives a unique durable row ID independent of caller-controlled trace metadata

A suitable shape is a server-generated spend-log primary key plus `litellm_call_id` as a separate indexed correlation field. If compatibility requires exposing the call ID through `request_id`, the stored identity still needs a server namespace or unique suffix

### Relevant code

- [Header assignment](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/common_request_processing.py#L1297)
- [Spend-log ID fallback](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/spend_tracking/spend_tracking_utils.py#L175-L183)
- [Primary-key schema](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/schema.prisma#L607-L610)
- [Duplicate-skipping insert](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/b1fd20f4cdc8f7a9b4e0c886a277465aedb05ec8/litellm/proxy/utils.py#L5782-L5813)

title: [Bug]: RejectedRequestError message prefixes leak into completion content
body:
## What happened?

`RejectedRequestError` is the proxy's mechanism for returning a message to the caller instead of
calling the model — `proxy_server.py` catches it and builds a response:

```python
except RejectedRequestError as e:
    _chat_response = litellm.ModelResponse()
    _chat_response.choices[0].message.content = e.message      # <- user-facing content
    ...
    return _chat_response
```

But `e.message` has been prefixed **twice** by the time it lands there, so the caller receives the
exception class names inside the completion text.

### Cause

`litellm/exceptions.py`:

```python
class RejectedRequestError(BadRequestError):
    def __init__(self, message, model, llm_provider, request_data, litellm_debug_info=None):
        self.status_code = 400
        self.message = "litellm.RejectedRequestError: {}".format(message)   # prefix #1
        ...
        super().__init__(message=self.message, ...)                          # prefix #2 in BadRequestError
```

Supplying `"366"` therefore delivers:

```json
{"choices":[{"message":{"content":"litellm.BadRequestError: litellm.RejectedRequestError: 366"}}]}
```

HTTP 200, correct latency, correct routing — only the text is wrong.

Class-name prefixes are right for an **error** surface. This value is used as **completion
content**, where they are not.

## Relevant log output

```
call 1: HTTP=200  time=4.500s     "content":"6"
call 2: HTTP=200  time=0.016s     "content":"litellm.BadRequestError: litellm.RejectedRequestError: 6"
call 3: HTTP=200  time=0.007s     "content":"litellm.BadRequestError: litellm.RejectedRequestError: 6"
```

## Reproduction

```python
# hook.py
from litellm.integrations.custom_logger import CustomLogger
from litellm.exceptions import RejectedRequestError

class Repro(CustomLogger):
    async def async_pre_call_hook(self, user_api_key_dict, cache, data, call_type):
        raise RejectedRequestError(
            message="366",
            model=str(data.get("model") or ""),
            llm_provider="",
            request_data=data,
        )

hook_instance = Repro()
```

```yaml
litellm_settings:
  callbacks:
    - hook.hook_instance
```

`POST /v1/chat/completions` returns 200 with content
`"litellm.BadRequestError: litellm.RejectedRequestError: 366"` rather than `"366"`.

## Suggested fix

Keep the raw text on the exception and use it for completion content, leaving the prefixed
`.message` for the error surface. For example, set `self.raw_message = message` in
`RejectedRequestError.__init__`, then in `proxy_server.py`:

```python
_chat_response.choices[0].message.content = getattr(e, "raw_message", e.message)
```

`getattr` keeps it backward-compatible with any other exception type reaching that handler.

Workaround for anyone hitting this today — restore the message after construction:

```python
err = RejectedRequestError(message=content, model=model, llm_provider="", request_data=data)
err.message = content
raise err
```

## Are you a ML Ops Team?

No.

## What LiteLLM version are you on?

`litellm 1.96.0` — `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:main-latest`,
digest `sha256:be646214d7bc1cda0be57debbbf58e822ca4f233ddc50d0c0c7fa9b4a28063af`

## Context

Found while implementing a response cache as a proxy callback. This is reachable **independently**
of the `str`-return path — we raise `RejectedRequestError` directly — so it affects any caller
using this public exception class to return a message.

Companion issue: the documented `str`-return contract is unreachable from `/v1/chat/completions`
because `acompletion` is missing from the call-type allowlist. Fixing that one **first and alone**
would route many more callers onto this defect.
author: johnpwhite

title: [Bug]: async_pre_call_hook `str` return is unreachable on /v1/chat/completions (call_type is `acompletion`)
body:
## What happened?

The proxy documents that returning a `str` from `async_pre_call_hook` gives the caller a message
instead of calling the model. `litellm/integrations/custom_logger.py` states it in the signature:

```python
async def async_pre_call_hook(
    self, user_api_key_dict: UserAPIKeyAuth, cache: "DualCache",
    data: dict, call_type: CallTypesLiteral,
) -> Optional[
    Union[Exception, str, dict]
]:  # raise exception if invalid, return a str for the user to receive - if rejected,
    # or return a modified dictionary for passing into litellm
```

On `POST /v1/chat/completions` that string reaches the client as an **HTTP 400 error** instead.

### Cause

`litellm/proxy/utils.py::process_pre_call_hook_response`:

```python
if isinstance(response, str):
    if call_type in ["completion", "text_completion"]:
        raise RejectedRequestError(
            message=response, model=data.get("model", ""),
            llm_provider="", request_data=data,
        )
    else:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail={"error": response})
```

`RejectedRequestError` is the good path — `proxy_server.py` catches it and returns a real
`ModelResponse` carrying the message as content (and handles streaming, with
`custom_llm_provider="cached_response"`).

But a normal chat request reaches the hook with **`call_type == "acompletion"`**, which is not in
that allowlist, so it takes the `else` branch and 400s. Logged from inside a callback on a live
proxy:

```
[pre_call] type='acompletion' keys=['model','temperature','messages','max_tokens','metadata','proxy_server_request']
```

The async call types (`acompletion`, and presumably `atext_completion`) appear to be missing,
which makes the documented behaviour unreachable on the main chat route.

## Relevant log output

```
raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail={"error": response})
fastapi.exceptions.HTTPException: 400: {'error': '0'}
```

```
call 1: HTTP=200  time=4.697s     (hook returned data -> model called)
call 2: HTTP=400  time=0.023s     (hook returned a str)
call 3: HTTP=400  time=0.018s
```

## Reproduction

```python
# hook.py
from litellm.integrations.custom_logger import CustomLogger

class Repro(CustomLogger):
    async def async_pre_call_hook(self, user_api_key_dict, cache, data, call_type):
        print(f"call_type={call_type!r}")
        return "hello from the hook"      # documented: the user receives this

hook_instance = Repro()
```

```yaml
litellm_settings:
  callbacks:
    - hook.hook_instance
```

`POST /v1/chat/completions` → **HTTP 400** `{"error":"hello from the hook"}`, and the log shows
`call_type='acompletion'`.

## Suggested fix

Include the async call types:

```python
if call_type in ["completion", "acompletion", "text_completion", "atext_completion"]:
```

Comparing against the `CallTypes` enum would be sturdier still, so a newly added call type cannot
silently fall through to the 400 branch.

> **Please fix this together with (or after) the companion issue on `RejectedRequestError` message
> prefixing.** On its own, this change routes every affected caller onto a path that currently
> delivers `"litellm.BadRequestError: litellm.RejectedRequestError: ..."` as the completion
> content — so fixing only this one would widen that defect's blast radius.

## Are you a ML Ops Team?

No.

## What LiteLLM version are you on?

`litellm 1.96.0` — `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:main-latest`,
digest `sha256:be646214d7bc1cda0be57debbbf58e822ca4f233ddc50d0c0c7fa9b4a28063af`

## Context

Found while implementing a response cache as a proxy callback, where a cache hit should
short-circuit and return the stored completion without calling the model. Only visible on a live
proxy — unit tests pass `call_type` themselves, so this cannot surface there.

Searched `RejectedRequestError`, `async_pre_call_hook` and `process_pre_call_hook_response` before
filing; #35281 is adjacent (dropped `post_call_failure_hook` return values on some routes) but a
different path.

title: [Bug]: Tag spend counters are not reseeded from durable database spend
body:
### Summary

When the Redis spend counter for a tag is missing or expires, `SpendCounterReseed.from_db()` intentionally returns `None` for `spend:tag:*`. The budget path then falls back to the cached `LiteLLM_TagTable.spend` value instead of reseeding from the authoritative tag row

### Current behavior

`litellm/proxy/db/spend_counter_reseed.py` documents that end-user and tag counters are excluded from DB reseeding. For tags, `from_db()` returns `None` immediately

`get_tag_objects_batch()` is cache-first. When a tag object is already cached on a worker, the object can contain a stale `spend` value after another worker has written spend or after a budget reset

`_tag_max_budget_check()` calls:

~~~python
tag_spend = await get_current_spend(
    counter_key=f"spend:tag:{tag_name}",
    fallback_spend=tag_object.spend or 0.0,
    max_budget=tag_object.litellm_budget_table.max_budget,
    fallback_authoritative=True,
)
~~~

On a clean Redis miss, the reseed path cannot query the tag row, and the stale cached `tag_object.spend` becomes the effective value

### Reproduction

Use a tag with a positive budget and two proxy workers:

1. Warm worker B's `tag:<name>` cache while its durable `spend` is low
2. Let worker A record spend for the same tag, or reset the tag budget in the database
3. Expire or delete Redis key `spend:tag:<name>`
4. Send a request carrying the tag through worker B

Worker B uses the cached tag row as the fallback instead of fetching the current durable spend. Depending on the stale direction, this can either allow requests after the tag budget has been exceeded or reject requests after a budget reset

### Impact

Tag budget enforcement can diverge across workers whenever the shared counter is cold and the per-worker tag object is stale. The failure is especially visible after Redis eviction, a new pod, a cache invalidation race, or a budget reset

Issue [#34238](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/34238) covers the corresponding end-user stale-fallback budget issue. This issue is the remaining tag-specific gap and should not be closed as a duplicate of the end-user report

### Expected behavior

Add a `spend:tag:` mapping to the authoritative reseed path, or force a fresh tag-row read when the Redis counter is missing. Cache invalidation after tag spend writes and budget resets should be coordinated with the fallback behavior

The implementation must preserve the zero-spend reset case and avoid double-incrementing a counter when multiple workers reseed it concurrently

### Source

- `litellm/proxy/db/spend_counter_reseed.py`, `SpendCounterReseed.from_db`
- `litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py`, `get_tag_objects_batch`
- `litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py`, `_tag_max_budget_check`
- `litellm/proxy/spend_tracking/budget_reservation.py`, tag counter setup

title: [Bug]: Spend entity updates are launched fire-and-forget and failures are swallowed
body:
### Summary

`DBSpendUpdateWriter.update_database()` awaits the spend-log insert but launches the user, key, team, organization, tag, agent, and daily spend updates with `asyncio.create_task()`. The returned coroutine completes before those updates run, and each helper failure is caught and logged at debug level inside the background task

### Current behavior

The writer contains:

~~~python
asyncio.create_task(
    self._batch_database_updates(...)
)
~~~

`_batch_database_updates()` runs the entity and daily update helpers sequentially, but wraps every helper in its own `try/except Exception` and only emits a debug message. The task is not retained by the writer for a later await, retry, or graceful-shutdown drain

The cost callback therefore treats `await update_database()` as completion even though the durable entity counters may not have been queued or written

This is different from the spend-log write failure covered by [#33873](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/33873), because the spend-log insert is awaited before this background task is created

### Reproduction

Patch one of the helper methods to fail and call `update_database()`:

~~~python
writer._update_team_db = AsyncMock(
    side_effect=RuntimeError("database unavailable")
)

await writer.update_database(
    token="sk-example",
    user_id="user-1",
    end_user_id=None,
    team_id="team-1",
    org_id=None,
    kwargs=request_kwargs,
    completion_response=response,
    start_time=start_time,
    end_time=end_time,
    response_cost=1.0,
)

# update_database() returns without propagating the failure
# the background task logs at debug level and the team update is lost
~~~

A second failure mode is process shutdown or request-scope task cancellation immediately after `create_task()`, before the task has enqueued any transaction

### Impact

Successful responses can be present in spend logs while one or more durable entity spend counters and daily aggregates are missing. Missing entity counters can understate budgets and reports, and a process restart can discard in-flight background tasks without a recovery record

### Expected behavior

Track the created task and drain it during shutdown, or use a durable queue whose enqueue operation is part of the awaited request path. Helper failures should be surfaced to a retryable queue, a failure metric, or a durable error record instead of being swallowed at debug level

The implementation should define whether a request is considered spend-accounted only after all required entity updates are queued durably

### Source

- `litellm/proxy/db/db_spend_update_writer.py`, `update_database`
- `litellm/proxy/db/db_spend_update_writer.py`, `_batch_database_updates`
- `litellm/proxy/hooks/proxy_track_cost_callback.py`, awaited writer call

title: [Security]: Responses ID security fails open for raw or ownerless response IDs
body:
### Summary

The Responses ID security hook only checks ownership when an ID can be decrypted into an encrypted LiteLLM response ID with nonempty owner metadata. Raw IDs and IDs returned unchanged after encryption setup fails bypass the ownership check, and an encrypted ID with empty user and team fields is accepted for every non-admin key

### Current behavior

The pre-call hook calls `check_user_access_to_response_id()` only when `_is_encrypted_response_id()` returns `True`. If decryption fails or the ID is not in the expected managed format, the hook forwards the ID without an ownership check

When `LITELLM_SALT_KEY` and `master_key` are both absent, `_encrypt_response_id()` logs at debug level and returns the provider response unchanged. This means a deployment with the security feature enabled can still return a raw response ID and later skip the security hook

The encrypted ID includes `user_api_key_dict.user_id or ""` and `team_id or ""`. The checker only rejects when either decoded field is truthy and differs from the caller. If both are empty, the function returns `True` for any non-admin caller

### Reproduction

The missing-key path can be exercised with `disable_responses_id_security` left at its default `False`, no `LITELLM_SALT_KEY`, and no `master_key`:

1. Make a successful Responses API request
2. Observe that the response ID is returned in its provider form because `_encrypt_response_id()` skipped encryption
3. Use a different valid LiteLLM key to retrieve, cancel, or list input items for that ID
4. The pre-call hook treats the raw ID as not encrypted and forwards it

The ownerless path can be tested directly:

~~~python
assert hook.check_user_access_to_response_id(
    response_id_user_id="",
    response_id_team_id="",
    user_api_key_dict=another_valid_key,
)
~~~

The assertion succeeds for a non-admin key even though no ownership relation was established

### Impact

A valid LiteLLM key can access another tenant's Responses API object when the provider ID is known or exposed, subject to the provider credential and endpoint behavior. Missing encryption configuration silently downgrades the feature from an ownership check to pass-through behavior

The security setting is enabled by default, so missing signing-key configuration should not silently disable its core guarantee

### Expected behavior

Fail startup or fail the Responses request when response ID security is enabled but no signing key is available. Every accepted response ID should have a verifiable ownership binding, or the proxy should perform a server-side ownership lookup for raw provider IDs

Treat an encrypted ID with no user and no team owner as invalid unless an explicit administrative or system path is being used

### Source

- `litellm/proxy/hooks/responses_id_security.py`, pre-call ID type gate
- `litellm/proxy/hooks/responses_id_security.py`, `check_user_access_to_response_id`
- `litellm/proxy/hooks/responses_id_security.py`, `_encrypt_response_id`
- `litellm/proxy/hooks/responses_id_security.py`, `_get_signing_key`

title: [Security]: Cached proxy-admin keys bypass blocked-key checks
body:
### Summary

A cached key whose role is `PROXY_ADMIN` returns from `user_api_key_auth()` before the normal `blocked` check. A stale local cache entry on another worker can therefore continue to authenticate after the key has been blocked in the database

### Current behavior

After loading a cached `UserAPIKeyAuth`, the proxy has a privileged early return for proxy-admin keys. That path checks expiration and updates request context, but it does not check `valid_token.blocked`

The ordinary non-admin path checks `valid_token.blocked` later

`block_key()` updates the database and attempts to delete the key from the local cache and the shared cache. The invalidation is not guaranteed to synchronously remove a stale entry from every worker. A worker that still serves the old cached admin object reaches the privileged early return and never consults the database

### Reproduction

Use two proxy workers with a shared database and cache:

1. Authenticate an admin key through worker B so its local cache contains `blocked=False`
2. Block the key through the management API or directly in the database
3. Make another request with the same key through worker B before its local cache refreshes
4. Observe that the request passes the admin early-return path, while a normal key would reach the blocked-key check

A focused test can construct a cached `UserAPIKeyAuth(user_role=PROXY_ADMIN, blocked=False)`, make the shared cache miss or stale, and assert that `user_api_key_auth()` does not authorize the key after an authoritative blocked record is present

### Impact

Blocking an admin key is not an immediate revocation guarantee across workers. The stale key can continue to access management and model routes for the cache lifetime or until invalidation succeeds

### Expected behavior

Run the blocked-key check before any privileged early return. For proxy-admin keys, either revalidate the blocked state against the database on every request or use a revocation version or generation that can be checked across workers without trusting the stale object

Add a multi-worker cache invalidation test that blocks a warmed admin key and verifies the next request is rejected

### Source

- `litellm/proxy/auth/user_api_key_auth.py`, cached `PROXY_ADMIN` early return
- `litellm/proxy/auth/user_api_key_auth.py`, normal blocked-key check
- `litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py`, `_delete_cache_key_object`
author: emerzon

title: [Bug]: Pass-through endpoints from raw config dicts skip centralized common checks
body:
### Summary

A pass-through endpoint supplied as a raw dictionary with no `auth` key still requires a valid LiteLLM key, but it silently skips the centralized common checks that an `auth: true` endpoint gets. Three call sites read the same `auth` field with two different defaults

This report has been rescoped. It originally claimed such an endpoint was completely unauthenticated. That is not true at HEAD, and I have removed the open-proxy framing. `create_pass_through_route()` puts `user_api_key_dict: UserAPIKeyAuth = Depends(user_api_key_auth)` in the generated handler's own signature, independent of the route-level `dependencies` list, and `check_api_key_for_custom_headers_or_pass_through_endpoints()` reads `endpoint.get("auth", True) is not True`. Both landed in `148485c2a2`, which closed GHSA-7h34-mmrh-6g58. I verified by registering the raw dict below against a `FastAPI` app: route-level `dependencies` is empty, but the resolved `route.dependant.dependencies` still contains `user_api_key_auth`

### Current behavior

`_register_pass_through_endpoint()` accepts either a `PassThroughGenericEndpoint` or a raw dictionary. For a Pydantic object, `model_dump()` materializes the default `auth=True`. For a raw dictionary, the registration code reads the field with no default:

~~~python
auth: Final[bool | str | None] = endpoint_data.get("auth")
dependencies = None
auth_enforced: Final = auth is not None and str(auth).lower() == "true"

if auth_enforced:
    dependencies = [Depends(user_api_key_auth)]
    if path not in LiteLLMRoutes.openai_routes.value:
        LiteLLMRoutes.openai_routes.value.append(path)
~~~

So `auth` omitted from a raw config gives `auth_enforced=False`, and the path is never appended to `LiteLLMRoutes.openai_routes`. `_run_centralized_common_checks()` then early-returns for that route, using a third reading of the same field that also has no default:

~~~python
if isinstance(endpoint, dict) and endpoint.get("path", "") == route and endpoint.get("auth") is not True:
    return
~~~

The net effect is a key-authenticated endpoint that never runs model-access checks, key/team/user budget checks, or route guardrails, because the proxy classifies it as an explicitly-unauthenticated forwarder

### Reproduction

~~~yaml
general_settings:
  pass_through_endpoints:
    - path: /internal/provider
      target: https://upstream.example.test
      # auth is omitted
~~~

An unauthenticated call is rejected, which is correct and is the part that changed since this issue was filed:

~~~bash
curl -i http://localhost:4000/internal/provider
# 401
~~~

A call with a valid key belonging to a fully exhausted budget succeeds anyway, because the centralized checks were skipped. Compare against the same config with `auth: true`, where the request is rejected on budget

### Impact

Model-access restrictions, budget enforcement, and guardrails are silently inert on any pass-through endpoint configured as a raw dict without an explicit `auth: true`. Authentication itself is intact, so this is a policy-enforcement gap rather than an exposure

### Expected behavior

Read the field consistently. Either normalize every endpoint through `PassThroughGenericEndpoint` before registration, or default the two remaining raw-dict reads to `True` so all three call sites agree:

- `pass_through_endpoints.py`, `_register_pass_through_endpoint`: `endpoint_data.get("auth", True)`
- `user_api_key_auth.py`, `_run_centralized_common_checks`: `endpoint.get("auth", True) is not True`

`tests/test_litellm/proxy/pass_through_endpoints/test_passthrough_auth_default.py` already covers the authentication default from the GHSA fix, so the new regression only needs to assert that a raw dict without `auth` reaches `_run_centralized_common_checks`

Related issues [#32202](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/32202) and [#26399](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/26399) discuss other pass-through security boundaries and do not duplicate this default mismatch

### Source

- `litellm/proxy/pass_through_endpoints/pass_through_endpoints.py`, `_register_pass_through_endpoint`
- `litellm/proxy/auth/user_api_key_auth.py`, `_run_centralized_common_checks` and `check_api_key_for_custom_headers_or_pass_through_endpoints`
- `litellm/proxy/_types.py`, `PassThroughGenericEndpoint.auth`
author: emerzon

title: [Bug]: Redis parallel request limiter falls back to per-pod limits on Redis errors
body:
### Summary

When the Redis-backed parallel request limiter cannot read or atomically acquire a slot, it falls back to an in-memory counter in the current process. In a multi-pod deployment this changes one configured global limit into an independent limit per pod

### Current behavior

`litellm/proxy/hooks/parallel_request_limiter_v3.py` uses Redis for the shared gauge and Lua acquisition. On exceptions it logs a warning and calls `_acquire_parallel_slots_in_memory()`

The in-memory fallback is process-local. With a configured limit of `N` and `R` proxy replicas, Redis failure can allow approximately `R * N` concurrent requests instead of `N`. A deployment with no Redis configured is a separate supported local-only mode; this issue concerns a deployment that configured Redis for cross-pod coordination and then loses Redis availability

### Reproduction

Configure a model or global parallel request limit and run two or more proxy replicas with Redis enabled

Inject Redis failures for both the gauge read and the atomic acquire:

~~~python
redis_client.eval = AsyncMock(side_effect=RuntimeError("Redis unavailable"))
redis_client.get = AsyncMock(side_effect=RuntimeError("Redis unavailable"))
~~~

Send requests concurrently to every replica. Each process admits up to the local limit because each process maintains its own fallback counter. The aggregate number of in-flight requests exceeds the configured shared limit

### Impact

A Redis incident can remove the cross-pod capacity guarantee and overload the upstream provider or local worker pool. This is especially risky when the limit is being used to protect a provider quota or a finite GPU capacity

The fallback is clearly an availability choice, but it should not be silent for configurations that depend on a shared limit

### Expected behavior

Add a configurable fail-closed mode for deployments that require a hard shared limit. If fail-open is retained, expose a health signal and metric showing that the limiter is running in per-pod degraded mode, and document the aggregate limit change

A safer fallback could use a bounded local limit derived from the replica count, but the system should not assume a replica count it cannot verify

### Related issues

Issue [#27900](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/27900) discusses global parallel request limit behavior. Issue [#34534](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/34534) discusses leaked parallel slots. Neither covers the Redis-error fallback changing a shared limit into per-pod limits

### Source

- `litellm/proxy/hooks/parallel_request_limiter_v3.py`, Redis gauge and acquire error paths
- `litellm/proxy/hooks/parallel_request_limiter_v3.py`, `_acquire_parallel_slots_in_memory`
author: emerzon

title: [Security]: JWT team_id_upsert creates arbitrary teams through a proxy-admin principal
body:
### Summary

When JWT authentication has `team_id_upsert` enabled, a signed JWT containing a team ID that is absent from the database can cause the proxy to create that team during request authentication. The upsert calls the normal team-creation endpoint with a synthetic `PROXY_ADMIN` principal

### Current behavior

`_get_team_db_check()` does the following when the team lookup returns no row:

~~~python
new_team_data = NewTeamRequest(team_id=team_id)
system_admin_user = UserAPIKeyAuth(user_role=LitellmUserRoles.PROXY_ADMIN)

created_team_dict = await new_team(
    data=new_team_data,
    http_request=mock_request,
    user_api_key_dict=system_admin_user,
)
~~~

The normal `new_team()` endpoint then skips non-admin team-limit checks and runs the creation flow as a proxy admin. The synthetic principal has no user ID and is not constrained to a pre-existing membership or team allowlist

The option defaults to `False`, but it is passed through the JWT team-claim resolution paths when enabled. Current hardening for provisional `x-litellm-team-id` headers does not remove this behavior for a genuine team claim in a signed JWT

### Reproduction

Configure JWT auth with team upsert enabled:

~~~yaml
general_settings:
  enable_jwt_auth: true
  litellm_jwtauth:
    team_id_jwt_field: tenant_id
    team_id_upsert: true
~~~

Use a valid token issued by the configured identity provider whose `tenant_id` is a previously nonexistent value such as `tenant-created-by-claim`. Send a normal model request. The authentication flow calls `_get_team_db_check()`, the team row is created through `new_team()`, and subsequent requests find the newly created team

The direct unit-level reproduction is to mock `TeamRepository.table.find_unique()` to return `None`, call `_get_team_db_check(..., team_id_upsert=True)`, and assert that `new_team()` receives `UserAPIKeyAuth(user_role=PROXY_ADMIN)`

### Impact

Any trusted identity-provider principal whose team or tenant claim is not constrained to an existing LiteLLM team can create rows and obtain a default team policy during ordinary authentication. This can cause team-row exhaustion and can turn an unprovisioned claim into an accepted team context

The JWT must still be valid and signed. This is an authorization and provisioning-boundary issue, not a JWT signature-forgery issue

### Expected behavior

Prefer requiring team IDs to be pre-provisioned and validating the claim against an explicit allowlist or membership mapping. If automatic provisioning is required, use a narrowly scoped provisioning path with bounded claims, safe default policy, audit metadata, and no broad proxy-admin authorization context

Add an integration test for a valid signed JWT with an unknown team claim and assert the configured policy for unknown teams, including whether the request is rejected or a restricted team is created

### Source

- `litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py`, `_get_team_db_check`
- `litellm/proxy/auth/handle_jwt.py`, JWT team resolution calls
- `litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/team_endpoints.py`, `new_team`
- `litellm/proxy/_types.py`, `LiteLLM_JWTAuth.team_id_upsert`
author: emerzon

title: [Bug]: In-memory spend transactions are lost when the database commit fails
body:
### Summary

The default non-Redis spend update path drains its in-memory queues before committing them to the database. If the commit fails, the drained transactions are not restored, so spend updates disappear

### Current behavior

The default for `use_redis_transaction_buffer` is `False`

`_commit_spend_updates_to_db_without_redis_buffer()` first calls:

~~~python
db_spend_update_transactions = await (
    self.spend_update_queue
    .flush_and_get_aggregated_db_spend_update_transactions()
)
await self._commit_spend_updates_to_db(
    db_spend_update_transactions=db_spend_update_transactions,
    ...
)
~~~

There is no `try/except` that restores the flushed batch when `_commit_spend_updates_to_db()` fails. The daily user, team, organization, end-user, and agent queues are flushed in the same method and are also not restored if their subsequent database update fails

Daily tag spend has the same defect in a sibling method. `_commit_daily_tag_spend_to_db()` flushes `daily_tag_spend_update_queue` and then calls `update_daily_tag_spend()` with no restore, so a failure there loses the batch too

The Redis-buffered sibling has since been hardened with an `uncommitted` dict and a `restore_transactions_to_redis` call in a `finally`, and `_drain_and_commit_daily_tag_spend_from_redis` got the same treatment. That leaves the default non-Redis path as the only one without any recovery

### Reproduction

A focused unit test can inject one transaction and force the commit to fail:

~~~python
queue = writer.spend_update_queue
await queue.add_update(transaction)

with patch.object(
    writer,
    "_commit_spend_updates_to_db",
    new=AsyncMock(side_effect=RuntimeError("database unavailable")),
):
    with pytest.raises(RuntimeError):
        await writer._commit_spend_updates_to_db_without_redis_buffer(
            prisma_client=prisma_client,
            n_retry_times=0,
            proxy_logging_obj=proxy_logging_obj,
        )

assert await queue.flush_and_get_aggregated_db_spend_update_transactions() == {}
~~~

The final assertion demonstrates that the failed batch has already been removed and is not available for a later retry. The same test shape can be applied to each daily queue

### Impact

A transient database outage, deadlock exhaustion, or process-level failure after the flush can permanently undercount key, user, team, organization, end-user, and daily spend in deployments using the default in-memory path

### Related issue

Issue [#33872](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/33872) covers the corresponding Redis-buffer loss and also discusses partial cross-entity commits. This report is the separate default in-memory path, where Redis cannot be used to replay the dequeued batch

### Expected behavior

Treat a flushed queue batch as in-flight until the database commit succeeds. On failure, restore the exact batch with an idempotency strategy, or use a durable outbox that can be retried without double counting

The recovery path should also cover each daily queue and should be exercised by failure-injection tests

### Source

- `litellm/proxy/db/db_transaction_queue/redis_update_buffer.py`, default setting
- `litellm/proxy/db/db_spend_update_writer.py`, `_commit_spend_updates_to_db_without_redis_buffer`
- `litellm/proxy/db/db_transaction_queue/spend_update_queue.py`

title: [Security]: Raw provider file IDs bypass managed-file ownership checks
body:
### Summary

The files retrieve, content, and delete endpoints enforce LiteLLM API-key authentication but do not enforce tenant ownership for raw provider file IDs. Managed unified IDs go through the managed-file hook, while any other provider file ID is forwarded to the provider using the current team's or shared provider credentials

### Current behavior

In `litellm/proxy/openai_files_endpoints/files_endpoints.py`:

- Unified managed IDs are routed through `ManagedFileRepository` and the managed-file hook
- Raw cloud-storage URIs are rejected
- Other raw IDs take the fallback branch, call `apply_team_provider_credentials()`, and invoke `litellm.afile_retrieve()`, `litellm.afile_content()`, or `litellm.afile_delete()`
- `validate_managed_files_requirement()` is currently used on the upload path and does not make retrieve, content, or delete reject raw provider IDs

If multiple tenants use the same provider account, knowledge of another tenant's provider file ID is enough to make the proxy ask the provider for that object under shared credentials. The provider may authorize the operation because it sees the shared account, not the LiteLLM tenant

### Reproduction

Use two LiteLLM teams that share provider credentials and a provider that accepts raw file IDs

1. Have team A create or otherwise obtain a provider file ID such as `file-abc123`
2. Authenticate as team B
3. Request `/v1/files/file-abc123`, `/v1/files/file-abc123/content`, and `DELETE /v1/files/file-abc123`
4. In a unit test, mock the three `litellm.afile_*` methods and assert that the raw ID reaches them without a managed-file ownership lookup

The same behavior applies when the raw ID is supplied through the provider-prefixed routes

### Impact

This can expose or delete another tenant's provider-backed file when provider credentials are shared across tenants. The attacker needs a valid LiteLLM key and a file ID, but the proxy's tenant boundary is not applied to this compatibility path

Related issues [#33989](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/33989) and [#28294](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/28294) discuss raw output file IDs from managed batch flows. They do not cover the generic files retrieve, content, and delete routes described here

### Expected behavior

Require a managed-file registration before retrieving, streaming, or deleting a file when multi-tenant isolation is enabled. Alternatively, make raw provider IDs an explicit compatibility opt-in and document that they are not tenant-isolated

The ownership check should cover all three operations, not only upload

### Source

- `litellm/proxy/openai_files_endpoints/files_endpoints.py`, `get_file_content`
- `litellm/proxy/openai_files_endpoints/files_endpoints.py`, `get_file`
- `litellm/proxy/openai_files_endpoints/files_endpoints.py`, `delete_file`

title: [Security]: End-user budget checks fail open on database lookup errors
body:
### Summary

A database error while loading an end-user object is converted into `None`, which is indistinguishable from an end user that was not found. The centralized authorization path then omits the end-user budget check

### Current behavior

`get_end_user_object()` catches a broad `Exception` and returns `None`

The common-check construction only adds `_check_end_user_budget()` when an end-user object with a budget is available. When the lookup failed because the database was unavailable, the result is the same as the not-found case and no budget check runs

This is separate from failures while reading a spend counter. The `fail_closed_budget_enforcement` setting cannot restore a check that was removed because object lookup returned `None`

### Reproduction

Create an end-user row with a positive `max_budget`, then inject a repository failure:

~~~python
from unittest.mock import AsyncMock, patch

with patch(
    "litellm.proxy.auth.auth_checks.EndUserRepository.table.find_unique",
    new=AsyncMock(side_effect=RuntimeError("database unavailable")),
):
    end_user = await get_end_user_object(
        end_user_id="existing-end-user",
        prisma_client=prisma_client,
        user_api_key_cache=user_api_key_cache,
        proxy_logging_obj=proxy_logging_obj,
    )
    assert end_user is None
~~~

Run the normal common-check path for the same request. Since the object is `None`, `_check_end_user_budget()` is not scheduled. A request can proceed even though the configured end-user budget could not be evaluated

### Impact

A transient database outage or repository exception can disable budget enforcement for requests attributed to affected end users. Repeated traffic can continue until the lookup succeeds again, and the failure is logged as a generic lookup failure rather than a policy denial

A genuinely missing end user may still be intentionally treated as unbudgeted, so the fix needs to distinguish not-found from infrastructure failure

### Expected behavior

Return a typed not-found result separately from a database or cache error. Infrastructure errors should either fail the request closed when a budgeted end user is expected, or use a clearly documented fallback that cannot silently remove the budget check

Add a test that makes `find_unique()` raise and asserts the request is denied or the error is surfaced instead of treating the user as absent

### Source

- `litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py`, `get_end_user_object`
- `litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py`, centralized common-check construction

title: [Bug]: Dynamic rate limiting allows traffic after unexpected check failures
body:
### Summary

The dynamic rate limiter is fail-open for unexpected errors. A Redis failure, cache exception, malformed counter response, or unexpected implementation error can make a request pass without dynamic rate-limit enforcement

### Current behavior

`_check_model_saturation()` catches every exception, logs it, and returns `0.0`, which represents an empty model

`async_pre_call_hook()` also catches every non-HTTP exception from the saturation and rate-limit checks, logs that it is allowing the request, and returns `None`

This is distinct from an intentional no-model-config case and from normal HTTP 429 handling

### Reproduction

Enable the dynamic rate limiter for a model with a configured RPM or TPM limit. In a unit test or failure injection environment, make either the saturation cache read or the rate-limit operation raise:

~~~python
limiter._get_saturation_value_from_cache = AsyncMock(
    side_effect=RuntimeError("Redis unavailable")
)
~~~

Call `async_pre_call_hook()` with a valid key and model. The hook returns `None` instead of rejecting or surfacing the infrastructure failure. If the error occurs in `_check_rate_limits()`, the outer exception handler has the same result

### Impact

During a Redis or cache incident, each request can bypass the configured dynamic model capacity. In a multi-worker deployment this can create a large burst of upstream traffic and defeat the priority allocation policy precisely when coordination is degraded

### Expected behavior

Provide a configurable fail-closed mode for production deployments, or make fail-open behavior require an explicit availability opt-in. At minimum, expose a health metric and rate-limited alert that distinguishes an infrastructure bypass from an ordinary allowed request

The behavior should be tested for both saturation-read failures and rate-limit increment failures

### Related issue

Issue [#23749](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/23749) discusses a different dynamic limiter fallback that affects model fallback behavior. It does not cover unexpected limiter errors allowing requests

### Source

- `litellm/proxy/hooks/dynamic_rate_limiter_v3.py`, `_check_model_saturation`
- `litellm/proxy/hooks/dynamic_rate_limiter_v3.py`, `async_pre_call_hook`

title: [Security]: Enabled drain endpoint accepts requests when no token is configured
body:
### Summary

Enabling the graceful drain endpoint without configuring a drain token makes `/health/drain` callable by any network-reachable client. A successful call starts process-wide shutdown and takes the worker out of rotation

### Current behavior

`health_drain()` intentionally does not use `user_api_key_auth` because Kubernetes `preStop` hooks commonly do not have proxy credentials

`_authorize_drain_request()` returns immediately when neither `general_settings.drain_endpoint_token` nor `DRAIN_ENDPOINT_TOKEN` is set:

~~~python
expected = _drain_endpoint_token()
if expected is None:
    return
~~~

The endpoint is therefore protected only by `enable_drain_endpoint`

### Reproduction

Enable the endpoint and omit the token:

~~~yaml
general_settings:
  enable_drain_endpoint: true
  # drain_endpoint_token is omitted
~~~

Then call it without credentials:

~~~bash
curl -i http://localhost:4000/health/drain
~~~

The request reaches `GracefulShutdownManager.start_shutdown()`, waits for the worker to drain, and causes readiness to fail until the process restarts. The endpoint is expected to be a `GET` route and may hold the client connection while draining

### Impact

Any caller able to reach the health port can trigger denial of service or repeatedly drain workers. This includes a misconfigured load balancer, a shared cluster network, or an internal service that can make arbitrary HTTP requests

The feature is disabled by default, which limits exposure, but the unsafe behavior begins as soon as an operator enables it without also configuring a secret

### Expected behavior

Fail closed when `enable_drain_endpoint` is true and no token is configured, preferably at startup or with a 401 response. If unauthenticated drain is required for a controlled environment, it should be an explicit separate opt-in rather than the implicit behavior of a missing secret

The deployment documentation and health probe examples should make the token requirement unavoidable

### Source

- `litellm/proxy/health_endpoints/_health_endpoints.py`, `_drain_endpoint_token`
- `litellm/proxy/health_endpoints/_health_endpoints.py`, `_authorize_drain_request`
- `litellm/proxy/health_endpoints/_health_endpoints.py`, `health_drain`

title: [Bug]: Custom auth skips centralized authorization and budget checks by default
body:
### Summary

When a custom authentication function returns a user object, the centralized common checks are skipped unless `custom_auth_run_common_checks` is explicitly enabled. The default is `False`, so custom auth integrations can authenticate a request while silently bypassing standard model, team, key, rate, and budget enforcement

### Current behavior

The custom auth builder returns its result directly to the auth pipeline. `_run_centralized_common_checks()` contains an early return equivalent to:

~~~python
if user_custom_auth is not None and not general_settings.get(
    "custom_auth_run_common_checks", False
):
    return
~~~

The code comments and startup warning explain that DB-backed checks are not run unless the operator opts in. A separate `enable_post_custom_auth_checks` setting covers a different post-auth hook and does not make the centralized common checks run

The same default behavior is duplicated in the WebSocket authentication helper, which makes the behavior dependent on two auth paths

### Reproduction

Configure a custom auth function and omit both common-check flags:

~~~yaml
general_settings:
  custom_auth: my_auth_module.authenticate
  # custom_auth_run_common_checks is omitted
  # enable_post_custom_auth_checks is omitted
~~~

Give the key or team a restrictive model allowlist or an exhausted budget. Return a valid `UserAPIKeyAuth` object from the custom auth function and send a request through a normal model route

The custom auth function succeeds, but the centralized checks that would enforce the DB-backed allowlist and budget are not run

### Impact

This is a security and configuration footgun for deployments that assume custom auth supplements LiteLLM's normal checks. A custom auth integration can unintentionally turn the proxy into an authenticated but unmetered or unrestricted forwarding layer

Custom auth may be intended to replace LiteLLM authorization entirely, so the issue is the unsafe default and contract ambiguity rather than the existence of the extension point

### Expected behavior

Make the secure behavior the default for custom auth, or require an explicit and prominently named opt-out for skipping common checks. The startup warning should identify every class of check that will be disabled and should make the effective policy unambiguous

At minimum, add an integration test showing the default behavior for a custom-authenticated request with an exhausted team or key budget

### Related issue

Issue [#25862](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/25862) discusses documentation for `enable_post_custom_auth_checks` and `custom_auth_run_common_checks`. It is related configuration context, but it does not duplicate this current default-enforcement concern

### Source

- `litellm/proxy/auth/user_api_key_auth.py`, `_run_centralized_common_checks`
- `litellm/proxy/auth/user_api_key_auth.py`, custom auth result handling
- `litellm/proxy/response_api_endpoints/endpoints.py`, WebSocket custom auth checks
