title: [Bug]: Auto Router ignores vision capability when picking a deployment, so one image permanently breaks a session
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

## What happens

If a model group (or an `auto_router` alias) mixes vision-capable and text-only deployments, one image kills the whole session, not just the turn it was sent on.

The client keeps the image in its history and resends it every turn. As soon as the router picks a text-only deployment, the provider rejects the entire request, so every following turn fails the same way. Client-side history compaction fails too, since it replays the full history, so there is no way out: the session has to be thrown away.

Hit this on Bedrock behind an `auto_router/complexity_router` alias, but nothing here is Bedrock-specific. Code below is the same on the `v1.94.0` tag and current `main`.

## Why

The router never looks at request modality when picking a deployment.

**1. `_pre_call_checks` has no modality filter.** `litellm/router.py:10163` filters candidates on context window, RPM, region, and unsupported params. That last one already does capability-based elimination via `litellm.get_supported_openai_params()`, but it is scoped to one param:

```python
special_params = ["response_format"]
for k, v in non_default_params.items():
    if k not in supported_openai_params and k in special_params:
        invalid_model_indices.add(idx)
```

There is no equivalent for image content, so a text-only deployment is never eliminated.

**2. `supports_vision` is not read anywhere in the routing path.** Grepping the repo (minus tests and `model_prices_and_context_window.json`), every hit is a type definition (`litellm/types/utils.py:141`, `litellm/types/router.py:574`), the public helper (`litellm/utils.py:2480`), model-hub aggregation in `Router.get_model_group_info` (`litellm/router.py:9105`), a Gemini prompt-template branch (`litellm/litellm_core_utils/prompt_templates/factory.py:5264`), or Fireworks (see below). Nothing in `router_strategy/`, `router_utils/pre_call_checks/` or `proxy/litellm_pre_call_utils.py`.

**3. The auto-router classifiers walk the content blocks, see the image, and drop it.** `AutoRouter._extract_text_from_messages` (`litellm/router_strategy/auto_router/auto_router.py:85`):

```python
if isinstance(content, list):
    return " ".join(
        block.get("text", "")
        for block in content
        if isinstance(block, dict) and block.get("type") == "text"
    )
```

`ComplexityRouter._extract_user_message_and_system_prompt` (`litellm/router_strategy/complexity_router/complexity_router.py:875`) applies the same `part.get("type") == "text"` filter. So the request gets classified as if it were text-only, and an image turn can land in a text-only tier.

**4. `session_affinity` (default true) then pins that deployment for the rest of the session.** That is what turns a one-off mismatch into a dead session rather than a bad turn.

**5. `drop_params` does not help.** It drops unsupported top-level params, not content blocks inside `messages`.

## The check already exists, for exactly one provider

`FireworksAIConfig` does this at the transformation layer (`litellm/llms/fireworks_ai/chat/transformation.py:326`):

```python
if content.get("type") == "image_url" and supports_vision_value is False:
    raise litellm.BadRequestError(
        message=f"Fireworks AI model {model} does not support image inputs. "
                "Use a Fireworks vision model or remove image_url content blocks.",
        model=model,
        llm_provider="fireworks_ai",
    )
```

It was never generalised, so on every other provider the request goes out and you get the provider's raw error back with no indication of which deployment was picked or what to change.

## What I would expect

Modality handled without breaking the session's model pin. That pin is what keeps provider-side prompt caches warm, and rerouting an image turn to a different deployment means the whole conversation prefix gets re-read cold by that model. In a long agentic session that is expensive, and it works against what `session_affinity` is there for in the first place.

So, in order:

**1. At pin time only.** When a session has no pin yet and the opening request already carries images, prefer vision-capable candidates within the classified tier. Nothing is cached at that point, so this costs nothing and loses nothing.

**2. Once a session is pinned, do not break the pin for modality.** Apply a configurable policy instead, for when the pinned deployment cannot take image content:

- `describe`: send the image, and only the image, to a cheap vision deployment, then inject the returned description in place of the image block. The machinery already exists in `_process_images` (`litellm/proxy/guardrails/guardrail_hooks/litellm_content_filter/content_filter.py:1396`), which already fans images out to a configured `image_model` via `llm_router.acompletion`. In a lot of setups the auto-router's own classifier model is already vision-capable, so no extra deployment is needed.
- `placeholder`: replace the image block with fixed text saying the model cannot see images, so it can tell the user rather than the request failing.
- `error`: today's behaviour, but raised by LiteLLM with the resolved deployment named, instead of passed through as a provider error. This is the Fireworks check above but generalised.

Descriptions and placeholder text have to be deterministic per image, so the description should be cached keyed on an image hash. While the image is the newest turn, injecting text there costs nothing cache-wise, but on later turns it sits mid-history, and wording that varies between turns invalidates the prompt cache from that point on.

All three policies need the router to know the request's modality in the first place, which is the piece that is missing. `supports_vision` is already on the deployment, it just is not consulted.

## Workaround

A proxy-side `async_pre_call_hook` that scans `data["messages"]` for image blocks and rewrites `data["model"]` to a vision-capable group. It works, but it is routing logic living outside the router, and it pays exactly the cost described above: the rerouted turn re-reads the entire conversation prefix cold on a model that has never seen the rest of the session.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure a model group / auto router mixing a vision-capable and a text-only deployment:

```yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: vision-model          # supports images
    litellm_params:
      model: bedrock/eu.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0
  - model_name: text-only-model       # no image support
    litellm_params:
      model: bedrock/<any text-only bedrock model>

  - model_name: smart-router
    litellm_params:
      model: auto_router/complexity_router
      complexity_router_config:
        tiers:
          SIMPLE:    text-only-model
          MEDIUM:    text-only-model
          COMPLEX:   text-only-model
          REASONING: vision-model
        session_affinity: true
      complexity_router_default_model: text-only-model
```

2. Open a session with a trivial first turn ("hi", "look at this repo") so it classifies `SIMPLE` and `session_affinity` pins the text-only model.

3. Send a follow-up turn with an image in it:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "smart-router",
    "messages": [
      {"role": "user", "content": "hi"},
      {"role": "assistant", "content": "hello"},
      {"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "text", "text": "what is in this image?"},
        {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "data:image/png;base64,<...>"}}
      ]}
    ]
  }'
```

4. You get the 400 below. Now send any further plain-text turn with the same history and it fails identically, because the image is still in `messages`. Compacting the history fails for the same reason, so the session cannot recover.

### Relevant log output

```shell
API Error: 400 litellm.BadRequestError: BedrockException - {"message":"This model doesn't support the image content block that you provided. Update the content bloc[k]...
Received Model Group=Smart Router
Available Model Group Fallbacks=None

# every subsequent turn in the same conversation returns the same error,
# including client-side history compaction:

Error during compaction: API Error: 400 litellm.BadRequestError: BedrockException - {"message":"This model doesn't support the image content block that you provi[ded]...
Group=Smart Router
Available Model Group Fallbacks=None
```

Proxy

title: Bedrock Converse silently ignores response_format={"type": "json_object"}
body:
# Bedrock Converse silently ignores `response_format={"type": "json_object"}`

## What happened

On Bedrock Converse, `response_format={"type": "json_object"}` is accepted,
produces no error, and has no effect on the request. The model answers in prose

The same request against an OpenAI model returns JSON, so callers writing
provider-agnostic code get a silent behaviour difference with no signal

## Reproduction

```python
import litellm

resp = litellm.completion(
    model="bedrock/converse/us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Who are you?"}],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)
```

**Expected:** a JSON object

**Actual:** prose, for example

```
I'm Claude, an AI assistant made by Anthropic. I'm here to help answer
questions, have conversations, and assist with various tasks.
```

The same call with a `json_schema` response_format does work

## Cause

`AmazonConverseConfig._translate_response_format_param`
(`litellm/llms/bedrock/chat/converse_transformation.py`) extracts a schema from
either `response_schema` or `json_schema`, then routes on it. A schema on a model
with native structured output support becomes `outputConfig`; a schema without
that support becomes a synthetic `json_tool_call` tool; no schema runs neither
branch

`{"type": "json_object"}` carries no schema, so it falls past both. The only
thing set is `optional_params["json_mode"] = True`, which is consumed on the
response-parsing side. Nothing reaches the outbound request, so the model is
never told to emit JSON

The net effect is that a parameter `get_supported_openai_params()` reports as
supported is dropped with no error and no warning

## Environment

- litellm `1.95.0` (code path unchanged in `1.89.2`)
- Model: `bedrock/converse/…anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5…`

title: [Bug]: Chat→Responses bridge omits required `annotations` field on `output_text` input items — strict Responses backends reject multi-turn requests
body:
### What happened?

When calling `/chat/completions` with a model backed by the Responses API, LiteLLM converts assistant history messages into Responses `input` items. The generated `output_text` content blocks do not include the `annotations` field:

```python
# litellm/completion_extras/litellm_responses_transformation/transformation.py
def _convert_content_str_to_input_text(self, content: str, role: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    if role == "user" or role == "system" or role == "tool":
        return {"type": "input_text", "text": content}
    else:
        return {"type": "output_text", "text": content}  # <-- no "annotations"
```

OpenAI's public API tolerates the missing field, but stricter Responses-compatible backends (e.g. Azure-style validators) reject the payload, since the `output_text` schema marks `annotations` as required:

```
litellm.BadRequestError: OpenAIException - {
  "error": {
    "code": "invalid_payload",
    "message": "Required property 'annotations' is missing",
    "param": "input[1].content[0].annotations",
    "type": "invalid_request_error",
    ...
```

The first turn works (no assistant history); every subsequent turn fails once an assistant message is replayed through the bridge.

### Repro

Two-turn `/chat/completions` call through the bridge against any Responses backend that enforces the spec:

```json
{
  "model": "<responses-backed model>",
  "messages": [
    {"role": "user", "content": "hi"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "hello"},
    {"role": "user", "content": "ping"}
  ]
}
```

The bridge produces `input[1] = {"role": "assistant", "content": [{"type": "output_text", "text": "hello"}]}` — missing `annotations` — and the upstream returns HTTP 400.

Also reproducible by POSTing the equivalent Responses-format payload (assistant `output_text` without `annotations`) directly; adding `"annotations": []` makes the same request succeed.

### Proposed fix

- Emit `"annotations": []` in the `output_text` branch of `_convert_content_str_to_input_text`.
- `item.setdefault("annotations", [])` for passthrough `output_text` items in `_convert_content_to_responses_format`.

Happy to open a PR.

Related but distinct: #18378 covered the reverse direction (Responses→Chat response translation dropping annotations).

### Relevant log output

```shell
litellm.BadRequestError: OpenAIException - {
  "error": {
    "code": "invalid_payload",
    "message": "Required property 'annotations' is missing",
    "param": "input[1].content[0].annotations",
    "type": "invalid_request_error",
    "details": [
      {
        "code": "ValidationError",
        "message": "Required property 'annotations' is missing",
        "param": "input[1].content[0].annotations",
        "type": "error",
        "details": []
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

v1.88.1 (also present on current `main`)

title: [Bug]: /v1/responses leaks rate-limiter metadata to upstream when RPM/TPM limits are configured
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate

### What happened?

Native `/v1/responses` requests gain a provider-visible top-level `metadata` parameter when the authenticated virtual key, user, team, project, organization, or agent has an RPM, TPM, or max-parallel-request limit that activates `parallel_request_limiter_v3`

The limiter stores `_litellm_proxy_rate_limit_response` by calling `_stash_value_in_metadata_channels()`. That helper writes to both `data["metadata"]` and `data["litellm_metadata"]`, and creates `data["metadata"]` when it is absent

For Responses API calls, `litellm_metadata` is the internal LiteLLM channel while `metadata` is a valid OpenAI Responses request parameter. The newly created `metadata` object therefore reaches the upstream provider. OpenAI-compatible backends that do not implement Responses metadata reject the request with HTTP 400

Expected behavior: rate-limit state remains internal and the upstream request body does not gain `metadata` unless the caller explicitly supplied provider metadata

Actual behavior: the upstream request contains metadata similar to the following and rejects it

```json
{
  "metadata": {
    "_litellm_proxy_rate_limit_response": {
      "overall_code": "OK",
      "statuses": [
        {
          "descriptor_key": "api_key",
          "rate_limit_type": "requests"
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

The regression was introduced by #32711, which began stashing `RATE_LIMIT_RESPONSE_KEY` for every successful rate-limit check. The underlying helper came from #27913

This is related to #28146, but it is a separate leak. That issue covered raw `_litellm_rate_limit_descriptors` and `_litellm_tpm_reserved_*` keys escaping at the top level. This issue covers the later `_litellm_proxy_rate_limit_response` value causing the entire Responses `metadata` provider parameter to be created

The relevant code is:

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/2c1d62ce2b586e047307c83d3ed79c64857287e8/litellm/proxy/hooks/parallel_request_limiter_v3.py#L2435-L2444

and:

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/2c1d62ce2b586e047307c83d3ed79c64857287e8/litellm/proxy/hooks/parallel_request_limiter_v3.py#L2766-L2780

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Run LiteLLM Proxy with a native Responses model pointing to an OpenAI-compatible backend that rejects the `metadata` Responses parameter

```yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: responses-model
    litellm_params:
      model: openai/responses-model
      api_base: os.environ/UPSTREAM_API_BASE
      api_key: os.environ/UPSTREAM_API_KEY

general_settings:
  master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY
  database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL
```

2. Generate a virtual key with an RPM limit

```bash
curl --request POST 'http://localhost:4000/key/generate' \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${LITELLM_MASTER_KEY}" \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{
    "models": ["responses-model"],
    "rpm_limit": 100
  }'
```

3. Call the native Responses endpoint using the generated key

```bash
curl --request POST 'http://localhost:4000/v1/responses' \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${LITELLM_VIRTUAL_KEY}" \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{
    "model": "responses-model",
    "input": "Reply with OK"
  }'
```

4. Observe that the upstream rejects a `metadata` parameter that was not present in the client request

5. Remove the key RPM limit or use a key without any applicable rate-limit descriptor and repeat the same request. The request succeeds because the limiter does not enter the `if descriptors:` branch and does not create top-level `metadata`

6. Alternatively, configure the deployment with the following workaround. The request succeeds because LiteLLM removes the leaked provider parameter before dispatch

```yaml
additional_drop_params:
  - metadata
```

title: [Bug]: OTel v2 promotes gen_ai.request.model onto non-LLM spans
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

### Actual behavior

OTel v2 includes `gen_ai.request.model` in the default `BAGGAGE_PROMOTED_KEYS`. `seed_request_identity()` then stamps that Baggage onto the FastAPI SERVER span and the Baggage processor copies it to DB, Redis, auth, guardrail, and other child spans.

Those spans are not generative AI operations, but they carry a canonical `gen_ai.*` model attribute. GenAI-aware backends can therefore classify the HTTP request, database, or service span as an LLM generation. With the Langfuse mapper this produces multiple apparent generations for one provider call and inflates/noises the observation hierarchy; the actual `LLM_CALL` span is the only span that should be a generation.

### Expected behavior

Canonical `gen_ai.request.model` should only be present on real GenAI operation spans. If the requested model needs to be propagated for correlation, it should use a LiteLLM vendor attribute such as `litellm.request.model` on non-LLM spans, or the vendor mapper should explicitly mark non-LLM roles as spans.

This must preserve user/team correlation and keep the real LLM-call span's existing `gen_ai.request.model` attribute.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Start LiteLLM v1.94.0 with `LITELLM_OTEL_V2=true` and the default `baggage_promoted_keys`.
2. Configure an in-memory or OTLP exporter and send one proxy completion request.
3. Inspect the raw exported SERVER, DB/service, and LLM-call spans.
4. Observe that `gen_ai.request.model` is present on the FastAPI SERVER span and non-LLM child spans because it was promoted through Baggage.
5. Send the trace to a GenAI-aware OTLP backend such as Langfuse and observe that non-LLM request/service operations can be rendered as generations instead of ordinary spans.

body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

### Actual behavior

When OTel v2 is configured with `mapper_names: [langfuse]`, `LangfuseMapper` emits generation model/usage/cost plus team metadata, but it does not map the standard Langfuse trace controls already supported by LiteLLM's existing Langfuse OTel integration:

- `trace_user_id` / end-user identity → `user.id` or `langfuse.user.id`
- `session_id` → `session.id` or `langfuse.session.id`
- `trace_name` → `langfuse.trace.name`
- request tags → `langfuse.trace.tags`
- explicitly approved trace metadata → `langfuse.trace.metadata.<key>`

As a result, native OTel v2 traces arrive in Langfuse with correct tokens and cost but without top-level user/session attribution, custom trace names, or tags. The same request fields are supported by `LangfuseOtelLogger._set_metadata_attributes` in the existing integration, so switching to the v2 mapper loses semantics.

### Expected behavior

The v2 Langfuse mapper should preserve the established LiteLLM Langfuse metadata contract using the current official Langfuse OTLP attribute names. Trace-wide attributes should be present on each relevant observation as recommended by Langfuse, while arbitrary metadata remains bounded by an operator allowlist.

This should not require enabling prompt/response content capture.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Start LiteLLM v1.94.0 with `LITELLM_OTEL_V2=true` and:

   ```yaml
   callback_settings:
     otel:
       exporter: in_memory
       mapper_names:
         - langfuse
       capture_message_content: no_content
   litellm_settings:
     callbacks:
       - otel
   ```

2. Send a completion request carrying the metadata controls supported by the existing Langfuse integration:

   ```json
   {
     "model": "test-model",
     "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hello"}],

       "trace_user_id": "user-1",
       "session_id": "session-1",

       "tags": ["test"]

   }
   ```

3. Inspect the exported LLM span attributes.

4. Observe `langfuse.observation.type=generation`, model, usage, and cost fields, but no mapped trace user, session, trace name, or tags.

title: [Bug]: OTel v2 drops allowlisted request metadata from boundary-born LLM spans
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

### Actual behavior

With `LITELLM_OTEL_V2=true`, metadata listed in `callback_settings.otel.baggage_metadata_keys` is missing from the normal proxy LLM-call span when that metadata is available in the final `StandardLoggingPayload` but was not part of the auth-time `UserAPIKeyAuth` object.

This is the common path because OTel v2 opens the LLM span in `log_pre_api_call`. At close, `RequestIdentity.from_payload()` contains the request/routing metadata, but `_close_llm_call()` calls `finish_span()` without applying the configured metadata allowlist. `_seed_identity_baggage()` is only used when span creation was deferred, so the same request can have different metadata depending on whether the span was opened at the boundary.

The configured allowlist therefore does not reliably produce `litellm.metadata.<key>` attributes. This also prevents vendor mappers such as Langfuse from receiving operator-approved late request/routing metadata.

### Expected behavior

Every key explicitly listed in `baggage_metadata_keys` should be stamped on the LLM-call span from the final typed payload, regardless of whether the span was created at pre-call or deferred until close. Unlisted metadata must remain excluded.

A narrow generic fix would apply the same allowlist to `LLMCallSpanData.identity.metadata` during `finish_span`/mapping, while retaining Baggage for propagation to spans that start after auth.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Start LiteLLM v1.94.0 with `LITELLM_OTEL_V2=true`, an in-memory or OTLP exporter, and:

   ```yaml
   callback_settings:
     otel:
       exporter: in_memory
       baggage_metadata_keys:
         - request_label
   litellm_settings:
     callbacks:
       - otel
   ```

2. Send a normal proxy completion request with primitive metadata that is present in the final logging payload but not in the auth object:

   ```json
   {
     "model": "test-model",
     "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hello"}],
     "metadata": {"request_label": "canary"}
   }
   ```

3. Inspect the exported LLM-call span.

4. Observe that `litellm.metadata.request_label` is absent on the boundary-born span, even though `request_label` is explicitly allowlisted and present in `LLMCallSpanData.identity.metadata` at close.

5. Force the deferred-span path and observe that the metadata seeding behavior differs.

title: [Bug]: MCP tool_name_to_display_name is ignored for config.yaml servers
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

### What happened?

`tool_name_to_display_name` and `tool_name_to_description` are ignored when an MCP server is configured through `config.yaml`.

The database/admin UI loading path appears to preserve these fields, but the YAML configuration loader does not pass them into the `MCPServer` object.

### LiteLLM version

Reproduced with:

- v1.91.0
- v1.94.0
- v1.95.0-rc.1
- current `main`

### Configuration

```yaml
mcp_servers:
  example_server:
    transport: http
    url: "http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp"
    auth_type: none
    allow_all_keys: true
    tool_name_to_display_name:
      example_tool: example_tool
```

The upstream MCP server returns:

```text
example_tool
```

LiteLLM returns:

```text
example_server-example_tool
```

### Expected behavior

LiteLLM should apply the configured display-name overrides and return:

```text
example_tool
```

The reverse mapping should continue routing calls to the original prefixed tools.

### Root cause

In `MCPServerManager.load_servers_from_config()`, the YAML loader constructs `MCPServer(...)` with fields such as:

```python
allowed_tools=server_config.get("allowed_tools"),
disallowed_tools=server_config.get("disallowed_tools"),
allowed_params=server_config.get("allowed_params"),
```

But it does not pass:

```python
tool_name_to_display_name
tool_name_to_description
```

The `MCPServer` model and runtime override/routing logic already support both fields.

### Suggested fix

Pass the fields when constructing config-defined MCP servers:

```python
tool_name_to_display_name=server_config.get("tool_name_to_display_name"),
tool_name_to_description=server_config.get("tool_name_to_description"),
```

A regression test should verify that overrides survive the `config.yaml` loading path and are reflected in `tools/list`.

### Additional context

The override feature was introduced in #22828.

Related feature requests #24102 and #26093 asked for a global option to disable MCP tool-name prefixing. Both were closed as stale/not planned. Issue #26093 also notes that `tool_name_to_display_name` is ignored in `config.yaml`.

This report is narrower and does not request disabling prefixing globally. It reports that the existing, supported override fields are dropped specifically by the `config.yaml` loading path.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Start an MCP server at `http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp` that exposes a tool named `example_tool`.

2. Create the following LiteLLM `config.yaml`:

```yaml
general_settings:
  master_key: sk-example-key-1234567890

mcp_servers:
  example_server:
    transport: http
    url: "http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp"
    auth_type: none
    allow_all_keys: true
    tool_name_to_display_name:
      example_tool: example_tool
```

3. Start LiteLLM:

```bash
litellm --config config.yaml --port 4000
```

4. Request the tool list:

```bash
curl --request POST \
  --url http://127.0.0.1:4000/mcp/example_server \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer sk-example-key-1234567890" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --header "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  --data '{
    "jsonrpc": "2.0",
    "id": 1,
    "method": "tools/list",
    "params": {}
  }'
```

5. Observe that LiteLLM returns:

```text
example_server-example_tool
```

6. The expected tool name, according to `tool_name_to_display_name`, is:

```text
example_tool
```

title: [Bug]: Bedrock batch file upload has no SSE-KMS support, blocking batch creation against KMS-enforced S3 buckets
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

Creating a Bedrock batch requires litellm to first upload the batch input file to S3. When the target S3 bucket enforces **SSE-KMS** (server-side encryption with a customer-managed KMS key) via bucket policy, the upload fails, because the KMS key configured on the credential is never passed through to the actual S3 `PutObject` call's encryption parameters.

**Best-effort root cause (please confirm/correct):** the KMS key field appears to be filtered out of the credential params object used for the batch file upload path (`CredentialLiteLLMParams` or equivalent) before it reaches the S3 upload call, so even when a KMS key is explicitly configured, it never makes it into the request.

### Impact

This is a **hard blocker**, not a minor inconvenience — for any organization whose S3 buckets require SSE-KMS by policy (as ours do), Bedrock batches cannot be created at all against those buckets, regardless of how the credential/model is configured. There is no workaround short of relaxing the bucket's encryption policy, which is not an option for us.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure a Bedrock batch model with S3 credentials pointing at a bucket whose policy requires `x-amz-server-side-encryption: aws:kms` with a specific KMS key ARN.
2. Attempt to create a Bedrock batch (which triggers litellm to upload the batch input file to that bucket first).
3. Observe the upload fails (S3 rejects the `PutObject` because the required KMS encryption header/param is missing), blocking batch creation entirely.

### Relevant log output

```
S3 PutObject rejected — bucket policy requires SSE-KMS, but the KMS key configured on the
credential is not present in the outgoing upload request.
```

### Expected behavior

The KMS key configured on the Bedrock/S3 credential should be passed through to the batch input-file upload's encryption parameters, so batches can be created against SSE-KMS-enforced S3 buckets.

### What happened?

Creating a Vertex AI batch with `vertex_location: global` is **accepted** at request time (no validation error), but litellm then builds a request URL using that location and forwards it to Vertex, which responds with an **HTTP 400** downstream. So `global` is silently accepted as if it were a valid Vertex region for batch operations, and the failure only surfaces well after the request has already been accepted — instead of failing fast with an actionable error, or being handled correctly.

**Best-effort root cause (please confirm/correct):** litellm's Vertex request-URL construction (which builds the per-region `*-aiplatform.googleapis.com` endpoint from `vertex_location`) doesn't special-case `global` for the batch surface the way some other Vertex AI endpoints do, so it builds a URL Vertex's batch API rejects.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure a Vertex AI model/`litellm_params` with `vertex_location: global`.
2. Create a batch via `POST /v1/batches` (or the SDK equivalent) against that model.
3. Observe the create call fails with an HTTP 400 from the downstream Vertex request, rather than either succeeding or being rejected up front with a clear "invalid location for batch" error at request-validation time.

Either: (a) `vertex_location: global` should be validated and rejected up front for batch operations with a clear, actionable error, or (b) if `global` is a legitimate value for some Vertex batch use case, litellm should translate it to whatever endpoint form the Vertex Batch Prediction API actually expects, rather than forwarding a URL that always 400s.

title: [Bug]: CheckResponsesCost background job never clears LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable rows stuck in queued
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

When using the Responses API with `background=true`, the resulting row in `LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable` gets stuck in `queued` status **permanently**, even after the response has actually completed at the provider. Confirmed on both Azure and native OpenAI deployments — same failure on both. In our environment we have 20+ rows stuck as `queued`, some dating back over two months.

Since the rows never transition out of `queued`, the `CheckResponsesCost` background job keeps picking them up on every polling cycle and fails the same way each time. This means:
- No cost is ever attributed for these background responses.
- The number of stuck rows only grows as more `background=true` requests come in, so wasted DB queries and log noise compound over time.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. `POST /v1/responses` with `background=true` (any model).
2. Poll `GET /v1/responses/{id}` until `status=completed`.
3. Check the DB:
   ```sql
   SELECT status FROM "LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable" WHERE file_purpose = 'response' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 5;
   ```
4. Observe the row is still `queued` — and stays that way through every subsequent `CheckResponsesCost` polling cycle, even though the provider has long since completed the response.

### Relevant log output

_No exception observed client-side — the response itself completes normally and is retrievable via `GET /v1/responses/{id}`. The bug is entirely in the background job's DB bookkeeping: the row's `status` column never advances past `queued`._

### Expected behavior

`CheckResponsesCost` should detect that the underlying response has completed at the provider, transition the `LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable` row out of `queued` to a terminal status, and compute/attribute cost exactly once — instead of leaving the row permanently `queued` and re-attempting it forever.

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

v1.89.1

title: [Bug]: afile_content calls are billed at 3x model_cost_per_token due to default-message-value placeholder
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

`afile_content` calls (retrieving file content — a files/storage API call, not an LLM completion) are billed a `response_cost`, even though there is no real token usage to bill. The cost consistently equals **exactly 3 × the model's `input_cost_per_token`** — e.g. for `vertex_ai/gemini-3-flash-preview` (`input_cost_per_token = 5e-07`), the recorded cost is `1.5e-6`, which is `3 × 5e-07`. This pattern appears across all `afile_content` calls where a response cost is recorded, regardless of the actual file size or content.

**Root cause:** `afile_content` is not a first-class, documented call type in `cost_calculator.py`'s Literal list and has no dedicated pricing rule. However, `afile_content` calls go through the same `@client` logging path as chat-style completions, and `HttpxBinaryResponseContent` is treated as a normal logged response — so the generic `response_cost` / `completion_cost` path still runs. Because `function_setup` never fills in real messages for this call type, it falls back to the placeholder string `"default-message-value"`, which gets stored as the logging input. Cost calculation then token-counts that placeholder string as the "prompt" — about 3 tokens with the standard tokenizer — and multiplies by the configured model's `input_cost_per_token`, giving exactly `3 × input_cost_per_token` for whatever model is on the log line. It is not tied to file size or actual inference; it's purely an artifact of the placeholder input being priced by generic per-token pricing.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure any model with a per-token `input_cost_per_token` rate.
2. Trigger an `afile_content` call (e.g. `litellm.afile_content(file_id=..., custom_llm_provider=...)`, or via any code path that downloads a file's content, such as a managed batch's output-file retrieval).
3. Check the resulting spend/cost log for that call (`response_cost` / the logged `StandardLoggingPayload`).
4. Observe `response_cost == 3 * input_cost_per_token` for the model on the log line, even though the call did not perform any LLM completion and has no real prompt/completion tokens.

### Relevant log output

```
Example: vertex_ai/gemini-3-flash-preview, input_cost_per_token = 5e-07
Observed response_cost for afile_content call: 1.5e-6  (== 3 * 5e-07)
```

### Expected behavior

`afile_content` (and any other non-completion call type that reaches this logging path without real usage) should not be priced via the token-based cost path at all — `response_cost` should be `0`, since there is no real token usage to bill. If there is a legitimate reason to charge for file retrieval, it should use a dedicated, documented pricing rule rather than accidentally token-pricing a placeholder string.

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

SDK (litellm Python package)

v1.89.1

title: [Bug]: /v1/messages to an OpenAI Responses model drops cached tokens (reads Anthropic-only usage keys) — cache reads billed at the full input rate
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

Closely related but distinct:
- #27763 (**closed, completed**) — the mirror-image defect: Anthropic-native `cache_read_input_tokens` not normalized into `prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens` for Vertex/Bedrock on `/v1/messages`. Same end symptom ("cache reads billed as full-priced input tokens"), opposite direction of translation. This report is the **OpenAI-backed** path, which was not covered by that fix.
- #11364 (`cached_tokens` not populated, Anthropic direct), #11789 (Anthropic streaming cost tracking ignores cache reads), #7790 (async logging callbacks drop cache fields when streaming).

### What happened?

When `/v1/messages` is routed to an OpenAI model (i.e. the Responses-API bridge, `_should_route_to_responses_api()` → `LiteLLMMessagesToResponsesAPIHandler` → `AnthropicResponsesStreamWrapper`), **cache-read tokens are always reported as 0**, even when OpenAI returns a large `cached_tokens` count.

Consequences:

1. The `message_delta` usage returned to the client omits `cache_read_input_tokens` entirely, so Anthropic-format clients (e.g. anything speaking the Messages API) display "no caching".
2. Anything downstream that prices from that usage bills **every cached prompt token at the full input rate**. For OpenAI, cached input is 10% of the input rate, so on a cache-heavy workload the computed cost is several times the real cost.

On our proxy this is stark and reproducible: the *same* model on the *same* day shows 89–95% cache-hit rates via `/responses` and **exactly 0.0%** via `/v1/messages`, every day. Long, stable-prefix agentic workloads are affected worst, since those are precisely the ones OpenAI caches best.

### User Flow

Before a (hypothetical) fix: cached tokens vanish whenever an Anthropic-format client is pointed at an OpenAI model, so users see no caching and spend reports overbill

1. A user points an Anthropic-format client (any Messages API SDK or tool) at the proxy and selects an OpenAI model that supports prompt caching
2. The client sends `POST /v1/messages` twice with the same long stable prefix (over 1024 tokens)
3. The second response streams a `message_delta` whose usage has no `cache_read_input_tokens`, so the client displays zero caching even though OpenAI served most of the prompt from cache
4. The proxy's spend logs and `/spend/logs` price every input token at the full rate, so the recorded cost for cache-heavy workloads runs several times the provider invoice

After a (hypothetical) fix: the same requests report the real cache split, so client usage and recorded spend match what OpenAI actually charged

1. The same client sends the same two `POST /v1/messages` calls
2. The second response's `message_delta` usage carries `cache_read_input_tokens` matching the `input_tokens_details.cached_tokens` the identical prompt reports on `POST /v1/responses`
3. Spend logs bill those tokens at the cache-read rate, and the recorded cost drops to the provider's actual charge

### Root cause

`litellm/llms/anthropic/experimental_pass_through/responses_adapters/streaming_iterator.py`, in `_process_event()` on the `response.completed` branch (line numbers from `main` today):

```python
242:  cache_creation_tokens = getattr(usage, "input_tokens_details", None)   # type: ignore[assignment]
243:  cache_read_tokens = getattr(usage, "output_tokens_details", None)      # type: ignore[assignment]
244:  # Prefer direct cache fields if present
245:  cache_creation_tokens = int(getattr(usage, "cache_creation_input_tokens", 0) or 0)
246:  cache_read_tokens = int(getattr(usage, "cache_read_input_tokens", 0) or 0)
```

`usage` here is an **OpenAI Responses** usage object. It does not have `cache_read_input_tokens` or `cache_creation_input_tokens` — those are Anthropic-native names. OpenAI reports:

- `usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens` — cache reads
- `usage.input_tokens_details.cache_write_tokens` — cache writes (a pydantic **extra**, so it survives `model_dump()` but is easy to miss)

So lines 245–246 evaluate to `0` on every OpenAI request, and the guarded assignments below never fire:

```python
263:  if cache_creation_tokens:
264:      usage_delta["cache_creation_input_tokens"] = cache_creation_tokens
265:  if cache_read_tokens:
266:      usage_delta["cache_read_input_tokens"] = cache_read_tokens
```

Note lines 242–243 look like a vestige of the correct intent: they read `input_tokens_details` / `output_tokens_details` into `int`-annotated variables and are then immediately overwritten by 245–246. The intent to consult `input_tokens_details` is there but the implementation was lost.

### Why the plain `/responses` path is not affected

`litellm/responses/utils.py` already does this correctly, which is exactly why only the Messages bridge is broken:

```python
1065:  cached_tokens=getattr(response_api_usage.input_tokens_details, "cached_tokens", None),
1069:  cache_write_tokens=getattr(response_api_usage.input_tokens_details, "cache_write_tokens", None),
```

The fix is to bring the Messages streaming adapter in line with this.

### Reproduction

**A. Deterministic, offline (no API key, no network).** This drives the real wrapper with an OpenAI-shaped `response.completed` event:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict
from litellm.llms.anthropic.experimental_pass_through.responses_adapters.streaming_iterator import (
    AnthropicResponsesStreamWrapper,
)

class Details(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="allow")   # cache_write_tokens arrives as an extra
    cached_tokens: int = 0

class Usage(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="allow")
    input_tokens: int
    output_tokens: int
    input_tokens_details: Details

class Response(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="allow")
    status: str = "completed"
    usage: Usage
    output: list = []

class Event(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="allow")
    type: str = "response.completed"
    response: Response

w = AnthropicResponsesStreamWrapper(responses_stream=iter([]), model="gpt-5.6-sol")
w._process_event(Event(response=Response(usage=Usage(
    input_tokens=12000, output_tokens=40,
    input_tokens_details=Details(cached_tokens=11008),
))))
delta = next(c for c in w._chunk_queue if c.get("type") == "message_delta")
print(delta["usage"])
```

Actual output on `main`:

```
{'input_tokens': 12000, 'output_tokens': 40}
```

Expected:

```
{'input_tokens': 12000, 'output_tokens': 40, 'cache_read_input_tokens': 11008}
```

**B. End-to-end.** `model_list` entry for any OpenAI model that supports prompt caching and the Responses API, then:

```bash
# Send the SAME request twice. OpenAI caches prefixes >= 1024 tokens automatically,
# so call 2 should report a large cached_tokens.
for i in 1 2; do
  curl -sS -X POST "http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/messages" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_KEY" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
    -d '{"model":"<openai-model>","max_tokens":64,"stream":true,
         "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"<paste >1024 tokens of stable text here> Reply with OK."}]}' \
  | grep -o '"usage":{[^}]*}' | tail -1
done
```

Observed: the second call's `message_delta` usage has no `cache_read_input_tokens`.
Control: the identical prompt sent to `/v1/responses` **does** report `input_tokens_details.cached_tokens`, confirming OpenAI cached it and only the Messages bridge loses the number.

### Suggested fix

Consult `input_tokens_details` when the Anthropic-native fields are absent, keeping the existing fields as first choice so Anthropic-backed callers are unaffected:

```python
                    cache_creation_tokens = int(
                        getattr(usage, "cache_creation_input_tokens", 0) or 0
                    )
                    cache_read_tokens = int(
                        getattr(usage, "cache_read_input_tokens", 0) or 0
                    )
                    # OpenAI Responses reports the cache split under
                    # input_tokens_details, not as Anthropic-native fields.
                    details = getattr(usage, "input_tokens_details", None)
                    details_dict: Dict[str, Any] = {}
                    if isinstance(details, dict):
                        details_dict = details
                    elif details is not None:
                        try:
                            details_dict = details.model_dump()
                        except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001
                            details_dict = {}
                    if not cache_read_tokens:
                        cache_read_tokens = int(details_dict.get("cached_tokens") or 0)
                    if not cache_creation_tokens:
                        cache_creation_tokens = int(
                            details_dict.get("cache_creation_tokens")
                            or details_dict.get("cache_write_tokens")
                            or 0
                        )
```

`model_dump()` matters: `cache_write_tokens` is a pydantic *extra*, so a fixed list of `getattr` reads can miss it depending on the SDK version.

There is a second half to this for spend logs. Any code path that synthesizes a `Usage` for logging from these counters must also populate `prompt_tokens_details`, or cost tracking still sees no cache split even after the above:

```python
usage = Usage(
    prompt_tokens=input_tokens,          # stays INCLUSIVE of cached tokens
    completion_tokens=output_tokens,
    total_tokens=input_tokens + output_tokens,
    prompt_tokens_details=PromptTokensDetailsWrapper(
        cached_tokens=cache_read_tokens or None,
        cache_creation_tokens=cache_creation_tokens or None,
    ),
)
```

`text_tokens` should be left unset: `generic_cost_per_token` derives the billable remainder as `prompt_tokens - cached - cache_creation`, so setting `text_tokens` as well double-counts, and setting `prompt_tokens` net-of-cache under-counts.

### Tests that should cover the fix

1. **`_process_event` maps OpenAI-shaped usage** — `input_tokens_details.cached_tokens=N` ⇒ `message_delta.usage["cache_read_input_tokens"] == N`. Parametrise `input_tokens_details` as both a pydantic model and a plain `dict`; both shapes reach this code.
2. **`cache_write_tokens` as a pydantic extra** is picked up and surfaces as `cache_creation_input_tokens` — guards against a `getattr`-list regression.
3. **Anthropic-native precedence preserved** — when `usage.cache_read_input_tokens` is set, the value is used unchanged and `input_tokens_details` is not consulted. No regression for Bedrock/Vertex.
4. **Absent cache fields ⇒ keys omitted** — no `cache_read_input_tokens: 0` appearing where it did not before.
5. **Cost regression test (the one that actually protects the bill)** — register a model with `input_cost_per_token`, `cache_read_input_token_cost`, `cache_creation_input_token_cost`, then assert `generic_cost_per_token` on the logged `Usage` equals
   `(input - cached - cache_write) * input_rate + cached * cache_read_rate + cache_write * cache_creation_rate`.
   With rates 5e-6 / 5e-7 / 6.25e-6 and 172k input / 155k cached / 3k cache-write, the expected input cost is **$0.166250**; the buggy path yields **$0.860000**. This test fails loudly on any regression that silently drops the cache split.
6. **Guard against zero-rating cache writes** — on a model with **no** `cache_creation_input_token_cost`, confirm cache-write tokens are not silently made free. `_calculate_input_cost` subtracts them from the billable input tokens and multiplies by a rate that defaults to `0`, so mapping them on a model that publishes no cache-write price turns paid tokens into free ones. (OpenAI currently prices cache writes only on its newest family; older models have no such rate.)

### Relevant log output

_No response_

### Are you a ML Ops Team?

No

### What LiteLLM version are you on?

Observed on v1.89.1; the offending code is unchanged on `main` as of this report (lines cited above).

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

_No response_

title: [Bug]: Streamed /v1/messages to an openai/ backend never emits a logging callback (AnthropicStreamWrapper / AnthropicResponsesStreamWrapper never thread litellm_logging_obj)
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

Streaming `POST /v1/messages` (Anthropic-format endpoint) routed to an `openai/`-provider backend returns HTTP 200 successfully and streams a correct Anthropic-shape SSE body to the client — but **no logging callback (`StandardLoggingPayload`) is ever emitted** for the request. The request is billed by the provider but recorded with 0 tokens / $0 cost, so it's invisible to any success-logging integration (spend tracking, S3/Datadog callbacks, etc). No exception is raised anywhere — this is a silent gap, not a crash.

This affects **both** of the custom Anthropic-messages streaming adapters:

| Adapter | Backend models | Streaming wrapper |
|---|---|---|
| `litellm/llms/anthropic/experimental_pass_through/adapters/` | chat-completions-API models (e.g. `gpt-4o-mini`) | `AnthropicStreamWrapper` |
| `litellm/llms/anthropic/experimental_pass_through/responses_adapters/` | Responses-API models | `AnthropicResponsesStreamWrapper` |

**Root cause:** Both `AnthropicStreamWrapper` and `AnthropicResponsesStreamWrapper` drain the inner provider SSE stream and translate/yield Anthropic-shape SSE bytes back to the client — but neither ever receives the `litellm_logging_obj`, and neither invokes the success-logging handler once the stream is fully consumed.

This is different from how litellm's other streaming paths behave:
- The standard `CustomStreamWrapper` (chat/responses) fires the success handler on stream completion.
- The Bedrock/Azure `BaseAnthropicMessagesStreamingIterator` (used for the *other* `/v1/messages` backends) also correctly fires logging on stream end.

Only the `openai/`-backend `/v1/messages` streaming path is missing this plumbing entirely — for both of its adapter variants.

**Expected behavior:** `litellm_logging_obj` should be threaded into both `AnthropicStreamWrapper` and `AnthropicResponsesStreamWrapper`, and the success-logging handler should fire once the SSE stream is fully consumed — mirroring `CustomStreamWrapper` / `BaseAnthropicMessagesStreamingIterator`.

**Related but distinct issues** (for context — neither is a duplicate of this): #28595 (closed, fixed by #28985) and #32487 both cover *crashes* in Responses-API logging on a different path (direct `/v1/responses`, or a pydantic `ValidationError` during result translation). This issue is a silent gap — no exception is ever raised, the success handler is simply never invoked.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure a `model_list` entry routed to an `openai/` provider backend (chat-completions or Responses API), e.g. `model_name: my-openai-model`, `litellm_params.model: openai/gpt-4o-mini`.
2. Register a success-logging callback (e.g. `litellm.callbacks = [...]`, or check `LiteLLM_SpendLogs` if using the proxy with a DB).
3. Send a streaming request to the Anthropic-format endpoint:
   ```bash
   curl -sS -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer <LITELLM_KEY>" \
     "http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/messages?beta=true" \
     -d '{"model":"my-openai-model","stream":true,"max_tokens":100,
          "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}'
   ```
4. Observe the client receives a normal streamed Anthropic-shape response (200 OK), but no `LiteLLM_SpendLogs` row is written and no logging callback fires for the request. Non-streaming `/v1/messages` to the same backend logs fine, and streaming `/v1/messages` to Bedrock/Azure backends also logs fine — only this combination (stream=true) x (/v1/messages) x (openai-provider backend) drops the log.

### Relevant log output

_No exception is raised — that's the bug. Nothing appears in logs to indicate the request was ever processed for logging purposes._

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.89.1

title: [Feature]: Generic tag-based rate limiting (token, request, and dollar caps per tag, with configurable windows)
body:
### The Feature

Add native support for **generic tag-based rate limiting**: a request-level tag identifies the caller (or any other logical entity), and the tag carries one or more configurable-window limits — **tokens, requests, or dollars** — enforced per routing attempt.

Concretely:
- A chain/model-group declares one grouping per unit (`token_limits` / `request_limits`
  / `dollar_limits`), and **each individual limit entry carries its own `tag_id`** — so
  even limits of the same unit on the same chain can key by different tags (e.g. a
  `daily` token limit per `end_user_id`, a `weekly` token limit per `team_id`), not
  just different tags per unit. **The window is declared in raw seconds
  (`period_seconds`), not a fixed day/week/month enum** — this is deliberate: it makes
  genuine sub-day windows (e.g. an RPM-style "5 requests per 60 seconds" cap per
  identity) expressible with the exact same mechanism as a daily/weekly/monthly one,
  not a separate feature:
  ```yaml
  model_info:
    token_limits:
      limits:
        - name: daily
          tag_id: end_user_id
          limit: 500000
          period_seconds: 86400
        - name: weekly
          tag_id: team_id
          limit: 2000000
          period_seconds: 604800
    request_limits:
      limits:
        - name: per_minute
          tag_id: end_user_id
          limit: 5
          period_seconds: 60
    dollar_limits:
      limits:
        - name: monthly
          tag_id: team_id
          limit: 50.0
          period_seconds: 2592000
  ```
  `period_seconds: 86400` (one day) resets exactly at UTC midnight, and `60` (one
  minute) resets on real clock-minute boundaries — any value that evenly divides a day
  aligns to a natural clock boundary the same way, since bucketing is just
  `epoch_second // period_seconds`.
- The caller sends the identity via the existing tag mechanism, e.g.
  `X-Litellm-Tags: end_user_id:<value>,team_id:<value>` (already native — tags are
  comma-split into `metadata.tags` in `litellm_pre_call_utils.py` before hooks run).
- Enforcement checks `sum(usage by that limit entry's tag value, in its grouping's
  unit, within its window) < limit` for every declared limit entry, rejecting with 429
  if any is exceeded — checked on **every routing attempt** (primary and each fallback
  hop), not just once before routing, so a fallback model group's own limits are
  enforced too.
- **Load-balanced groups** (multiple `model_list` entries sharing one `model_name`,
  evaluated as simultaneous alternatives) need an explicit answer for what a limit
  means when more than one deployment is behind it — this isn't a corner case, it's a
  property of `Router.model_list` itself. Proposal: if every deployment sharing a
  `model_name` declares the *identical* value for a given limit, it's enforced as ONE
  shared, chain-wide bucket (the common case — a limit meant to apply to the group
  regardless of which member serves the request); if deployments genuinely declare
  *different* values, each gets its own independent bucket, and a breach on either
  still rejects the whole routing attempt (it does **not** filter just that deployment
  out and let the router try a sibling in the same group — simpler, and avoids a
  caller silently succeeding against limit config they didn't actually satisfy). A
  naive first implementation that just indexes by `model_name` and keeps whichever
  deployment it sees first will silently drop divergent config with no error — worth
  flagging explicitly since it's exactly the mistake the validated in-house
  implementation shipped with initially, caught only when directly asked "chain level
  or model level?"

Example request, under the limit:
```bash
curl http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Litellm-Tags: end_user_id:user-123" \
  -d '{
    "model": "gpt-4o",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hello"}]
  }'
# -> 200, and user-123's configured counters (tokens/requests/dollars,
#    per declared window) are incremented by the real usage from the response.
```

Same request once `user-123` is at/over any configured limit (e.g. the 6th request
within 60 seconds against the `per_minute` limit above):
```bash
curl http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Litellm-Tags: end_user_id:user-123" \
  -d '{
    "model": "gpt-4o",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hello"}]
  }'
# -> 429
# {
#   "error": {
#     "message": "tag_rate_limit_exceeded",
#     "type": "requests",
#     "tag_id": "end_user_id",
#     "tag_value": "user-123",
#     "limit_name": "per_minute",
#     "limit": 5,
#     "period_seconds": 60
#   }
# }
```

A request with no matching tag (or a different tag id than the one the model group is
configured for) would pass through unaffected — the limit only applies to identities
that actually send it.

### Motivation, related issues

Today, no single mechanism covers all three combinations of (arbitrary tag-based identity) × (configurable window) × (choice of unit):

- **Tag budgets** (`/tag/new`, `_tag_max_budget_check`) are **dollar-only**, and the reset window is whatever the tag budget system supports — not a per-tag-declared list of independent windows.
- **`tpm_limit`/`rpm_limit`** are token/request-based, but hard-coded to a rolling **~1-minute** window (env-configurable via `LITELLM_RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_SIZE`, but process-global, not per-limit) — there's no way to configure a daily/weekly cap, and no way for two different limits on the same key/tag to use two different windows at once.
- **`max_budget`/`budget_duration`** (user/key/customer) support a genuine, configurable daily/weekly/etc. reset window — but only for **dollars**, and only for entities **provisioned in LiteLLM's own DB** (users/keys/customers), not for an arbitrary caller-supplied tag value that doesn't have a LiteLLM key of its own.

This proposal covers both ends at once — a single `period_seconds`-based mechanism handles a genuine per-minute RPM-style cap *and* a daily/weekly/monthly cap, for tokens, requests, or dollars, keyed by an arbitrary tag — rather than needing `tpm_limit`/`rpm_limit` for the short-window case and a separate mechanism for longer windows.

This design has already been implemented and live-verified as an in-house proxy hook (token/request/dollar limits, per-entry `tag_id`, `period_seconds`-based windows including a genuine 5-requests-per-60-seconds case, per-hop enforcement, and both shared and per-deployment enforcement for load-balanced groups, verified against real load balancing across two real deployments) — happy to share more detail on the validated design if useful for review.

title: [Feature]: Native Multi-Tenancy & Tenant Isolation for Vector Storage / RAG Endpoints
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### The Feature


## 💡 Proposed Solution

We propose introducing **Vector Multi-Tenancy Configuration** in `config.yaml` and header-based tenant routing inside LiteLLM Proxy.

### 1. Header-Based Tenant Identification
Allow LiteLLM Proxy to extract tenant identity from configurable incoming request headers or JWT claims:
* `x-tenant-id` / `x-client-id`
* Bearer token claims (`tenant_id`)

### 2. Tenant Vector Isolation Modes
Support two primary industry-standard multi-tenancy models:

#### Mode A: Index / Collection / Corpus Name Prefixing (Hard Isolation)
Automatically partition vector stores and cloud RAG engines by prefixing index, collection, or corpus names with the resolved `tenant_id`:
```
Target Index/Corpus = {tenant_prefix}_{requested_index}
Examples:
  • OpenSearch / PGVector / Qdrant: tenant_52149_clinical_docs_index
  • Azure AI Search: tenant-52149-clinical-docs-index
  • Vertex AI RAG Engine: projects/{project}/locations/{region}/ragCorpora/tenant_52149_{corpus_id}
```

#### Mode B: Automatic Metadata Filter Injection (Soft Isolation / Shared Index)
For shared vector collections or corpora, automatically append a top-level metadata filter to all vector search and RAG retrieval calls (`/vector/search`, `/rag/search`):
```json
// Incoming proxy payload to /rag/search or /vector/search:
{ "query": "clinical protocols", "top_k": 5 }

// Transformed payload forwarded to Vector DB / Cloud RAG Engine:
{
  "query": "clinical protocols",
  "top_k": 5,
  "filter": { "tenant_id": { "$eq": "tenant_52149" } }
}
```

### 3. Proposed `config.yaml` Schema

```yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: enterprise-vector-search
    litellm_params:
      model: opensearch/dev-vector-cluster
      api_base: "https://search-domain.us-east-1.es.amazonaws.com"

  - model_name: vertex-rag-service
    litellm_params:
      model: vertex_ai/rag_engine
      vertex_project: "my-gcp-project"
      vertex_location: "us-central1"

  - model_name: azure-ai-search-service
    litellm_params:
      model: azure_ai_search/clinical-index
      api_base: "https://my-search.search.windows.net"

router_settings:
  vector_multitenancy:
    enabled: true
    tenant_header_key: "x-tenant-id"       # Header containing tenant identifier
    isolation_strategy: "index_prefix"     # Options: "index_prefix" | "metadata_filter" | "strict_mapping"
    metadata_tenant_key: "tenant_id"        # Field name for Mode B filtering
    
    # Supported Endpoints: /vector/ingest, /vector/search, /rag/ingest, /rag/search
    endpoints:
      - "/vector/ingest"
      - "/vector/search"
      - "/rag/ingest"
      - "/rag/search"
    
    # Optional: Explicit Tenant Mapping Table
    tenant_mappings:
      tenant_52149:
        allowed_indices: ["clinical_docs", "research_papers"]
        allowed_rag_corpora: ["corpus_clinical_v1"]
        rate_limit_rpm: 1000
      tenant_89123:
        allowed_indices: ["finance_reports"]
        rate_limit_rpm: 500
```


---

## 🔍 Alternatives Considered

1. **Upstream Application Isolation (Current Workaround)**: Each microservice implements its own DB lookup and presigns index names or filter payloads before sending requests to LiteLLM Proxy.  
   * *Drawback:* Duplicates auth logic across dozens of microservices and creates a risk of cross-tenant data leakage if an application omits a filter.
2. **Multiple Proxy Instances per Tenant**: Deploying a dedicated LiteLLM Proxy container instance per tenant.  
   * *Drawback:* High operational overhead, poor resource utilization, and complex deployment management at enterprise scale.

---

## ➕ Additional Context & Enterprise Benefits

* **Security & Compliance**: Guarantees zero cross-tenant data contamination at the gateway layer (SOC2 / HIPAA compliance requirement).
* **Unified Telemetry**: Enables Prometheus/Datadog metrics breakdown of Vector DB QPS and latency per tenant (`litellm_vector_requests_total{tenant_id="xxx"}`).
* **Seamless Integration**: Aligns LiteLLM’s existing model multi-tenancy and virtual key features with vector database access.

---

### Priority / Impact
* **Impact:** Critical for enterprise RAG deployments, multi-tenant SaaS platforms, and centralized AI gateways handling sensitive partitioned data.


### Motivation, pitch


## 🚀 Problem Statement

As enterprises adopt LiteLLM Proxy as a unified AI Gateway, vector database and managed RAG endpoints (e.g., **OpenSearch**, **Pinecone**, **Qdrant**, **Milvus**, **PGVector**, **Vertex AI RAG Engine**, and **Azure AI Search**) are increasingly routed through the proxy alongside completion and embedding endpoints via `/vector/ingest`, `/vector/search`, `/rag/ingest`, and `/rag/search` API routes.

However, LiteLLM Proxy currently lacks native **multi-tenancy abstraction for Vector Storage & RAG Endpoints**. When routing document ingestion (`/rag/ingest`) or semantic search (`/rag/search`) requests through the proxy, there is no standardized gateway mechanism to:

1. **Enforce Tenant Namespace/Index Isolation**: Prevent Tenant A from querying or overwriting vector indices, collections, or corpora belonging to Tenant B across vector databases or managed cloud RAG services (e.g. Vertex AI RAG Corpus, Azure AI Search Index).
2. **Inject Mandatory Tenant Metadata Filters**: Automatically append tenant scoping filters (e.g., `tenant_id: "tenant-123"`) to vector queries (`/vector/search` or `/rag/search`).
3. **Per-Tenant Vector Rate Limiting & Metrics**: Track vector query/ingestion throughput and apply rate limits (RPM/QPS) grouped by tenant ID across `/rag/ingest` and `/rag/search` endpoints.

Without this, downstream services are forced to build custom sidecar middleware to map tenant credentials to isolated indices, corpora, or metadata filter clauses, negating the central management benefits of LiteLLM Proxy.

Proxy

title: feat(router): required-AND tag routing via & prefix
body:
## Problem

Tag routing today supports inclusion-OR (`tag_filtering_match_any`, default `true` — a deployment matches if it carries *any one* of the request's positive tags) and independent negation (`!tag`, #31728). There's no way to express "must match all of these tags" — required-AND — per request. `tag_filtering_match_any` is a single router-wide setting, not overridable per request, so there's no way for one caller to get AND semantics while another gets OR on the same proxy.

This matters for intent/preference-style routing that combines multiple independent dimensions in one request — e.g. "give me a high-reasoning model AND specifically from Anthropic" (`reasoning_type:high` + `provider:anthropic`). Under today's OR semantics, that request instead returns *any* deployment matching either tag — e.g. a low-reasoning Anthropic model, or a high-reasoning non-Anthropic model — silently broader than what was asked for.

Separately: when tag constraints (`!` negation today, or the `&` proposal below) eliminate every candidate deployment on a model group, behavior is currently fixed — fall back to the `"default"`-tagged pool if any deployment has it, otherwise raise `no_deployments_with_tag_routing`. Different model groups want different behavior here: a group used for a compliance-driven exclusion (e.g. "never route to Provider X for this account") needs a hard failure when the exclusion can't be honored, since silently falling back would mean the exclusion only holds when it isn't actually load-bearing. A group used for a soft routing preference (e.g. `reasoning_type:high`) should degrade gracefully instead of erroring the whole request. There's currently no way to configure this per model group — it's one fixed behavior for everyone.

## Proposed solution

**1. `&` prefix for required-AND inclusion**, alongside the existing plain (OR) and `!` (negate) prefixes:

```
x-litellm-tags: &reasoning_type:high,&provider:anthropic
```

A deployment must carry every `&`-tagged value to match. This composes with existing plain tags (further OR-narrowing among survivors) and `!` negation (still applied first, unconditionally):

```
x-litellm-tags: &reasoning_type:high,provider:anthropic,provider:openai,!inference:cerebras
# must be high-reasoning, AND (anthropic OR openai), AND not cerebras-hosted
```

Values stay literal (not regex), consistent with the existing negation feature's ReDoS-avoidance rationale.

**2. Per-model-group configurable fail-open/fail-closed behavior.** A new `model_info` field (naming open to maintainer preference, e.g. `tag_filtering_strict`) settable per model group, controlling what happens when `!` negation or the proposed `&` requirement eliminates every deployment in that group:

```yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: compliance-critical-chain
    litellm_params:
      model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6
      tags: ["provider:anthropic"]
    model_info:
      tag_filtering_strict: true   # hard-fail (raise no_deployments_with_tag_routing) if a constraint can't be honored
  - model_name: soft-preference-chain
    litellm_params:
      model: openai/gpt-4o
      tags: ["provider:openai", "reasoning_type:low"]
    # tag_filtering_strict unset -> falls back to the "default"-tagged pool instead of erroring
```

We think this is more useful as an explicit per-group opt-in than a single router-wide setting, since a proxy commonly serves both compliance-sensitive chains and best-effort/preference-routed chains at the same time, and today's single fixed behavior can't serve both well.

## Open questions worth discussing

- Which default is safer to ship: keep today's fail-closed behavior as the default for `!` (so existing users relying on hard-fail-on-empty aren't silently affected) and let `tag_filtering_strict` opt a group *out* into fail-open, or make fail-open the new default (better fit for the `&` use case, which is entirely new) and let the flag opt a group *into* strict? We lean toward not silently changing `!`'s existing default given it may be load-bearing for other users' access-control use cases today, but want maintainer input given the backwards-compatibility tradeoffs either way.
- Should `tag_filtering_strict` live on `model_info` (checked once per model group) or as a `router_settings`-level default with a per-group override? Per-group `model_info` mirrors how other per-group behaviors are already configured in this codebase, but happy to align with whatever convention fits LiteLLM's existing patterns best.
author: deepanshululla

title: UI: show the model family logo in the models table, not just the provider's
body:
## The problem

On a proxy that routes many models through a single aggregating provider, every row in the models table shows the **same** logo — the provider's. That makes the list visually uniform and hard to scan, even though the models come from very different families.

Concretely, with ~20 Scaleway models configured, every row shows the Scaleway mark, whether the model is Mistral Small, Qwen3, Gemma, Llama 3.3, GPT-OSS, GLM or Whisper. The same happens with any aggregator: OpenRouter, Together, Bedrock, SageMaker, Groq, Fireworks, DeepInfra, Novita.

Scaleway's own console solves this by showing the **model family** icon rather than its own: Mistral rows get the Mistral mark, Qwen rows the Qwen mark, Gemma the Google mark, and so on. It makes a twenty-row list readable at a glance.

## Why this looks cheap to do

Two things are already in place:

1. **The assets exist.** `ui/litellm-dashboard/public/assets/logos/` already ships `mistral.svg`, `qwen.png`, `google.svg`, `meta_llama.svg`, `openai_small.svg`, `deepseek.svg`, `anthropic.svg` — the families that aggregators mostly serve.

2. **The precedent exists.** `providerLogoMap` already maps some entries to a *family* logo rather than the hosting provider's:

   ```ts
   [Providers.CODESTRAL]: mistralLogo.src,
   [Providers.TEXT_COMPLETION_CODESTRAL]: mistralLogo.src,
   [Providers.SageMaker]: bedrockLogo.src,
   ```

   So "the logo names the model family" is already an accepted idea in this file — it's just not reachable from a model name.

## Suggested shape

A resolver that looks at the model id first and falls back to today's behaviour, so nothing regresses:

```ts
// provider_info_helpers.tsx
const modelFamilyLogoMap: Array<[RegExp, string]> = [
  [/(^|\/)mistral|ministral|codestral|pixtral|devstral|voxtral/i, mistralLogo.src],
  [/(^|\/)qwen/i, qwenLogo.src],
  [/(^|\/)gemma|gemini/i, googleLogo.src],
  [/(^|\/)llama/i, metaLlamaLogo.src],
  [/(^|\/)gpt|whisper/i, openaiLogo.src],
  [/(^|\/)deepseek/i, deepseekLogo.src],
  [/(^|\/)claude/i, anthropicLogo.src],
];

export const getModelLogo = (model: string, provider: string): string =>
  modelFamilyLogoMap.find(([motif]) => motif.test(model))?.[1]
  ?? getProviderLogoAndName(provider).logo;
```

Callers that render a model row switch from `getProviderLogoAndName(provider).logo` to `getModelLogo(model, provider)`. Callers that render a *provider* row — cost tracking, provider margins — keep the current function untouched.

## Open questions for maintainers

- **Is this wanted at all?** It's a deliberate change of meaning for the icon in the models table: from "who serves it" to "what it is". Both are defensible, and it's your call which one the table should answer.
- **Regex vs. explicit map.** A regex list is short and covers unseen variants; an explicit map is predictable but needs updating for every new model. The sketch above uses regex with a provider fallback, so an unmatched model is never worse off than today.
- **Should the provider stay visible somewhere?** A tooltip, or a small provider badge on the family icon, would keep both facts. That's more work and probably a second step.

I'm happy to open the PR if the direction is agreed — I'd rather check the design first than send an unsolicited change to a shared component.

For reference, #35094 adds the missing Scaleway provider logo, which is the narrow fix for the specific case that surfaced this.

title: anthropic-request-id dropped on streaming /v1/messages (anthropic_messages call_type)
body:
## Bug

When using the `/v1/messages` endpoint with `stream: true` (call_type `anthropic_messages`), the upstream Anthropic response headers — including `anthropic-request-id` — are dropped and never reach `_hidden_params["additional_headers"]`.

### Root cause

The streaming logging path (`streaming_iterator._handle_streaming_logging` → `PassThroughStreamingHandler._route_streaming_logging_to_handler` → `anthropic_passthrough_logging_handler._build_complete_streaming_response`) rebuilds the `ModelResponse` from SSE events only. The raw `httpx.Response` (with all upstream headers) is already stashed at `model_call_details["httpx_response"]` (`llm_http_handler.py:2081`), but `_handle_anthropic_messages_response_logging` returns the assembled `ModelResponse` in the stream branch without stamping `_hidden_params["additional_headers"]` from it.

### Impact

- `StandardLoggingPayload.hidden_params.additional_headers` is `null` for all streaming `anthropic_messages` calls.
- The Anthropic `request_id` (`req_...`) is unreachable from SpendLogs, OTEL spans, and custom callbacks — making it impossible to correlate content-filter blocks, refusals, or other streaming outcomes with Anthropic-side request ids.
- The non-streaming path and the `/chat/completions` path are NOT affected — they already capture headers via `AnthropicConfig.transform_response`.

### Reproduction

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:4000/v1/messages   -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY"   -H "anthropic-version: 2023-06-01"   -H "content-type: application/json"   -d '{"model":"claude-sonnet-4-20250514","max_tokens":64,"stream":true,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}'
```

Then check the OTEL span or SpendLogs row — `hidden_params.additional_headers` will be `null`.

### Expected behaviour

`_hidden_params["additional_headers"]` should carry `llm_provider-anthropic-request-id` (and all other `llm_provider-*` headers) on streaming `anthropic_messages` calls, same as the non-streaming path.

title: [Feature]: Support deployment-level cost discounts
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### The Feature

Support an optional deployment/model-level `cost_discount` field in custom pricing metadata.

Example proxy/router config:

```yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: gpt-4o-mini-discounted
    litellm_params:
      model: openai/gpt-4o-mini
      api_key: os.environ/OPENAI_API_KEY
    model_info:
      id: discounted-deployment-1
      cost_discount: 0.8
```

`cost_discount` would be a float between `0` and `1`, where `0.8` means an 80% discount is applied to the calculated base cost. The final reported cost would be `base_cost * (1 - cost_discount)`.

### Motivation, pitch

LiteLLM already supports provider-level discounts through `cost_discount_config`, but some deployments need accurate spend tracking for negotiated or deployment-specific pricing without changing the shared base model price.

Today, operators can override input/output token prices per deployment, but there is no generic way to say "use the normal built-in model pricing, then apply this deployment's discount." This makes it harder to model negotiated pricing, reseller pricing, and per-deployment commercial terms while keeping the model cost map clean.

Desired behavior:

- Allow `cost_discount` in deployment `model_info` and custom pricing params.
- Apply deployment/model-level `cost_discount` before falling back to provider-level `cost_discount_config`.
- Keep deployment-specific discounts isolated from shared backend model pricing entries.
- Continue stripping client-supplied pricing controls at the proxy boundary unless an operator explicitly allows pricing overrides.
- Validate `cost_discount` is between `0` and `1`.

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

SDK (litellm Python package), Proxy
