title: [Bug] MCP server UI omits "authorization" auth_type — backend supports it, dropdown does not
body:
### What happened

The backend accepts `auth_type: "authorization"` for MCP servers (sends the credential verbatim as the `Authorization` header), but neither the **Create** nor **Edit** MCP server UI form exposes it in the auth-type dropdown. It's only reachable via the management API (`POST`/`PUT /v1/mcp/server`).

### Why it matters

Servers that require an `Authorization` header with a scheme other than the presets (`Bearer`/`Basic`/`token`) can't be configured from the UI. Concrete case: **Elastic Kibana Agent Builder MCP** (`/api/agent_builder/mcp`) requires `Authorization: ApiKey <key>`. The UI's `api_key` option sends `X-API-Key: <key>` instead (intentional, per the form's own hint text), so the upstream returns `401`. Only `auth_type: authorization` with the value `ApiKey <key>` works, and that's UI-unreachable.

### Evidence (current `main`)

- Backend enum + Literal accept it: `litellm/types/mcp.py:36` (`authorization = "authorization"`), `:61` (in `MCPAuthType`)
- Client builds the header: `litellm/experimental_mcp_client/client.py:435-436` -> `headers["Authorization"] = self._mcp_auth_value`
- UI enum missing it: `ui/litellm-dashboard/src/components/mcp_tools/types.tsx` (`AUTH_TYPE` has none/api_key/bearer_token/token/basic/oauth2/aws_sigv4)
- Dropdowns missing it: `ui/litellm-dashboard/src/app/(dashboard)/mcp-servers/_components/create_mcp_server.tsx:1075-1082`, `mcp_server_edit.tsx:1115-1122`

### Suggested fix

Add `AUTHORIZATION: "authorization"` to the `AUTH_TYPE` constant and a `<Select.Option value="authorization">Authorization (raw header)</Select.Option>` to both dropdowns; include it in `AUTH_TYPES_REQUIRING_AUTH_VALUE` so the value field shows.

title: [Bug]: Bedrock tool_config cache injection point invisible in logging callbacks (Langfuse) — only message-level cache_control is logged
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

When using Bedrock prompt caching with a tool-level cache injection point (cache_control_injection_points with location: "tool_config", see [LiteLLM docs — Anthropic Cache Control (Bedrock)](vscode-file://vscode-app/Applications/Visual%20Studio%20Code.app/Contents/Resources/app/out/vs/code/electron-browser/workbench/workbench.html)), the cache marker is correctly sent to Bedrock — confirmed by real [cache_creation_input_tokens](vscode-file://vscode-app/Applications/Visual%20Studio%20Code.app/Contents/Resources/app/out/vs/code/electron-browser/workbench/workbench.html) and [cache_read_input_tokens](vscode-file://vscode-app/Applications/Visual%20Studio%20Code.app/Contents/Resources/app/out/vs/code/electron-browser/workbench/workbench.html) values in the API response, and this matches Bedrock's documented request format for caching tool definitions (see [AWS Bedrock — Prompt caching, "tools checkpoints" example](vscode-file://vscode-app/Applications/Visual%20Studio%20Code.app/Contents/Resources/app/out/vs/code/electron-browser/workbench/workbench.html)). However, this cache marker never appears in logging/observability integrations (e.g. [Langfuse](vscode-file://vscode-app/Applications/Visual%20Studio%20Code.app/Contents/Resources/app/out/vs/code/electron-browser/workbench/workbench.html) traces).

This is inconsistent with system/message-level caching: when a cache injection point targets a system prompt or message, the cache marker is visible in the trace (e.g. Langfuse shows the message with its cache annotation). For tools, the equivalent marker is silently missing from the trace, even though it was genuinely applied and genuinely produced cache hits/misses (per [AWS Bedrock's usage fields for prompt caching](vscode-file://vscode-app/Applications/Visual%20Studio%20Code.app/Contents/Resources/app/out/vs/code/electron-browser/workbench/workbench.html), cacheReadInputTokens/cacheWriteInputTokens).

Expected: Tool-level cache markers should be visible in logging/tracing output, the same way message-level cache markers are.

Actual: Tool-level cache markers are invisible in logging callbacks. The only way to confirm tool caching is working is by inspecting usage.cache_creation_input_tokens/ usage.cache_read_input_tokens on the raw API response — tracing tools give no visibility into it.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Call Bedrock (e.g. anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6) with tool calling, adding cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"} to the last tool (or cache_control_injection_points with location: "tool_config").
2. Send the request twice. Confirm usage.cache_creation_input_tokens (1st call) and usage.cache_read_input_tokens (2nd call) are non-zero, proving caching worked.
3. Check the Langfuse trace for either call: the tools section shows no cache annotation, unlike when caching a system message (location: "message"), which does show one.

title: AttributeError: dict object has no attribute usage in Responses API streaming
body:
When using `/v1/responses` with streaming, three code paths access `.response.usage` without checking if the response is a dict. Some upstream providers return dict-format responses, causing `AttributeError` in all three locations.

**Affected files:**

1. `router.py` `_extract_partial_responses_usage` — `return completed.response.usage` crashes when `completed.response` is a dict. Causes HTTP 500 mid-stream.

2. `litellm_logging.py` `_get_assembled_streaming_response` — `isinstance(result.response.usage, ResponseAPIUsage)` crashes for the same reason. Tagged `[Non-Blocking]` but silently drops the log entry — successful requests never appear in SpendLogs.

3. `transformation.py` `translate_responses_chunk_to_openai_stream` — `for item in output_items` crashes when `output_items` is None. Triggers when a client calls `/chat/completions` but upstream only supports `/responses` (LiteLLM bridges the format, then crashes during back-conversion).

**Fix:** Add `isinstance(response, dict)` guards before attribute access, and `or []` for None iterable. PR follows.

**Version:** v1.93.0 (`main-stable`)

body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

When general_settings.store_prompts_in_spend_logs: true is enabled in LiteLLM v1.93.0, the config is successfully loaded from the mounted config.yaml, but prompt content is still not persisted into LiteLLM_SpendLogs.messages.
I verified this with fresh requests after restart.
Observed behavior:
acompletion rows have messages = {}
aresponses rows also have messages = {}
response is populated, but messages remains empty
this happens even after confirming the config is present both on the host and inside the container
Expected behavior:
when store_prompts_in_spend_logs: true is enabled, prompt/input content should be stored in spend logs
at minimum, LiteLLM_SpendLogs.messages should contain the request messages for /chat/completions
if prompt data is intentionally stored in another field, that should be documented clearly
This does not appear to be a UI-only issue. Direct SQL inspection of LiteLLM_SpendLogs shows messages is actually persisted as {}.

### Steps to Reproduce

1.Run LiteLLM v1.93.0 via Docker with this config:
general_settings:

title: [Bug]: MCP DCR bridge forwards lowercase bearer token type and causes upstream 401
body:
## What happened?

An `oauth_delegate` server with `dcr_bridge: true` can complete DCR, PKCE authorization, and token exchange successfully but return zero tools because the bridge copies the upstream OAuth `token_type` value verbatim into the protected-resource Authorization header.

A standards-based remote MCP provider returns `token_type: "bearer"` in lowercase. LiteLLM seals that value and later emits `Authorization: bearer <token>` from `resolve_bridge_envelope`. This provider treats the scheme casing strictly and returns HTTP 401 `invalid_token`.

A provider-neutral direct DCR/PKCE probe using the exact same token proved:

- `Authorization: bearer <token>` -> MCP initialize HTTP 401, `invalid_token`
- `Authorization: Bearer <token>` -> MCP initialize HTTP 200
- tools/list -> HTTP 200 with 32 tools

No token value is logged; the probe correlates attempts by a truncated SHA-256 fingerprint.

## Expected behavior

Canonicalize a case-insensitive OAuth token type of `bearer` to the interoperable `Bearer` scheme before protected-resource egress. RFC 6749 defines the token type value as case insensitive. Other token types can remain unchanged.

Minimal change in `outbound_credentials/bridge_credentials.py`:

```python
authorization_scheme = (
    "Bearer" if grant.token_type.lower() == "bearer" else grant.token_type
)
upstream_authorization = (
    f"{authorization_scheme} {grant.access_token.get_secret_value()}"
)
```

## Version

Reproduced on LiteLLM commit `bae22aad7cfe09d0ef0e41ec12cf1c7d9d0cbbb2`, used by the in-progress DCR bridge canary.

title: [Feature]: Add upstream quota and balance probing
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### The Feature

Add an optional, capability-based SDK interface for proactively querying quota or balance information reported by an upstream provider. This should be distinct from LiteLLM's configured budgets and spend observed by the proxy.

A possible interface:

```python
snapshot = await litellm.aprobe_provider_quota(
    model=model,
    api_key=api_key,
    api_base=api_base,
)
```

with a normalized result along these lines:

```python
ProviderQuotaSnapshot(
    provider="openrouter",
    scope="credential",       # credential/account/project/subscription
    unit="usd",               # usd/tokens/requests/percent
    limit=25.0,
    used=6.5,
    remaining=18.5,
    resets_at=None,
    as_of=...,
)
```

Suggested implementation:

- Add an optional `probe_quota` capability to provider configurations; unsupported providers return `None` or a typed `NotSupported` result.
- Reuse LiteLLM's provider resolution and credential handling rather than requiring callers to detect providers.
- Implement adapters only where providers expose a supported API, potentially starting with OpenRouter's `/api/v1/key` endpoint.
- Normalize only common fields while retaining provider/scope/unit so semantically different quotas are not presented as equivalent.
- Cache results for a short configurable TTL, apply strict timeouts, and never include credentials in results or logs.
- Expose the capability through the Python SDK first, with an optional authenticated Proxy endpoint later.
- Keep this separate from `/provider/budgets`: that endpoint represents configured LiteLLM policy and LiteLLM-observed spend, while this capability represents an upstream provider snapshot.

### Motivation, pitch

Applications need to know that a credential or subscription is nearly exhausted before starting a long or expensive task. A normalized probe would allow gateways to route proactively, UIs to show remaining allowance, and clients to avoid retrying a provider whose billing quota cannot recover through backoff.

LiteLLM's current spend and budget facilities only account for traffic observed by LiteLLM. They cannot reflect usage outside LiteLLM, promotional credits, provider-side adjustments, or purchased quota packages. Downstream projects therefore either add provider-specific HTTP calls or wait for a request to fail and parse provider-specific errors.

Related work exists, but leaves this gap: #18242 requested upstream usage/limits and was closed stale; #31823 proposes provider quota pools and package-aware routing; and #32785 addresses reactive insufficient-quota classification. This proposal provides the proactive provider capability those use cases could build on without making every downstream project implement its own provider registry.

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

SDK (litellm Python package)

No

title: [Bug]: Concurrent router budget-window resets can overwrite spend
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I searched open and closed issues before filing
- [x] I found no existing issue for last-write-wins spend resets in `RouterBudgetLimiting`

### What happened?

When a provider, deployment, or tag budget window is considered expired, `_handle_new_budget_window` resets the spend key with a plain `SET` to the current response's cost

Concurrent responses crossing the same window boundary can all enter the reset path. Each writes only its own cost, so the final counter contains whichever write wins instead of the sum of all response costs

The start-time and spend keys are also written separately, so another worker can observe a mixed window state. In multi-replica deployments this directly undermines the shared budget counter at the point where traffic crosses a budget boundary

A separate reliability concern in the same accounting path is that queued Redis increments are dispatched with `asyncio.create_task` and the queue is cleared immediately, so the sync method does not wait for the remote write to complete

The reproduction uses synthetic cache keys, timestamps, and costs and makes no provider or network call

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Check out commit `24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c`
2. Run this script from the repository root

```python
import asyncio

from litellm.caching.caching import DualCache
from litellm.router_strategy.budget_limiter import RouterBudgetLimiting


async def main():
    # Construct only the helper state to avoid starting its periodic task
    limiter = object.__new__(RouterBudgetLimiting)
    limiter.dual_cache = DualCache()

    await asyncio.gather(
        limiter._handle_new_budget_window(
            spend_key="provider_spend:synthetic:1h",
            start_time_key="provider_budget_start_time:synthetic",
            current_time=1000.0,
            response_cost=0.05,
            ttl_seconds=3600,
        ),
        limiter._handle_new_budget_window(
            spend_key="provider_spend:synthetic:1h",
            start_time_key="provider_budget_start_time:synthetic",
            current_time=1000.0,
            response_cost=0.07,
            ttl_seconds=3600,
        ),
    )

    stored = await limiter.dual_cache.async_get_cache(
        "provider_spend:synthetic:1h"
    )
    print(
        {
            "stored_spend": stored,
            "additive_expected": 0.12,
        }
    )


asyncio.run(main())
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
{'stored_spend': 0.07, 'additive_expected': 0.12}
```

The exact winner is scheduling-dependent. It may be `0.05` or `0.07`, but cannot correctly become `0.12` because the reset operation is assignment rather than accumulation

The direct helper call isolates the boundary operation. In normal flow, every response that reads the same expired `budget_start` can enter this helper concurrently

### Current-code analysis

Budget start time is read and initialized with separate cache operations rather than an atomic window claim

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/router_strategy/budget_limiter.py#L340-L351

The reset helper sets spend to one response cost, then sets start time in a second operation

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/router_strategy/budget_limiter.py#L353-L375

The expired-window branch calls that helper after a non-atomic read and comparison

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/router_strategy/budget_limiter.py#L446-L496

Provider, deployment, and tag success accounting all converge on `_increment_spend_for_key`, so the race is shared by each budget type

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/router_strategy/budget_limiter.py#L401-L444

Redis pipeline work is started in the background and the local queue is cleared without awaiting the write

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/router_strategy/budget_limiter.py#L525-L548

### Suggested correction

Make window selection and spend accumulation one atomic operation in the shared backing store

One option is a Redis Lua script that identifies the active window, initializes it only when absent or expired, adds the response cost with `INCRBYFLOAT`, and applies the matching TTL to the window metadata and counter before returning the new total

A window identifier embedded in the spend key can avoid mixing a late increment from the old window into a newly reset counter

The in-memory path needs equivalent locking for the same logical key. Redis pipeline pushes should copy the pending operations, await the pipeline result, and clear or requeue only after success

Regression coverage should synchronize two reset calls at the boundary and assert additive spend for provider, deployment, and tag budgets, including a two-instance Redis case and pipeline failure/retry behavior

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

SDK Router and Proxy Router budgets

title: [Bug]: Concurrent requests can bypass max_budget_per_session before spend is recorded
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I searched open and closed issues before filing
- [x] I found no existing issue for the check-then-increment race in `max_budget_per_session`

### What happened?

The session budget hook checks accumulated spend before a request, but does not reserve any budget during admission. Actual response cost is added only after each successful request

Two or more requests for the same session can therefore read the same below-budget value and all pass. Their eventual combined cost can exceed `max_budget_per_session` by a multiple of request concurrency

The post-response Redis increment is atomic, but that only makes the final overage accurately visible. It does not make the preceding admission decision atomic and does not prevent the overage

This is especially relevant to parallel agent turns and multi-replica proxy deployments, which are the scenarios where a session-scoped budget needs cross-request coordination

The reproduction uses synthetic agent, key, session, budget, and cost values and makes no provider or network call

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Check out commit `24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c`
2. Run this script from the repository root

```python
import asyncio
from unittest.mock import patch

from litellm.caching.caching import DualCache
from litellm.proxy._types import UserAPIKeyAuth
from litellm.proxy.hooks.max_budget_per_session_limiter import (
    _PROXY_MaxBudgetPerSessionHandler,
)
from litellm.proxy.utils import InternalUsageCache
from litellm.types.agents import AgentResponse


async def main():
    cache = DualCache()
    handler = _PROXY_MaxBudgetPerSessionHandler(
        InternalUsageCache(cache)
    )
    auth = UserAPIKeyAuth(
        api_key="sk-synthetic",
        agent_id="agent-synthetic",
    )
    agent = AgentResponse(
        agent_id="agent-synthetic",
        agent_name="synthetic-agent",
        litellm_params={"max_budget_per_session": 0.10},
        agent_card_params={
            "name": "synthetic-agent",
            "version": "1",
        },
    )
    data = {
        "model": "gpt-4.1",
        "metadata": {"session_id": "session-synthetic"},
    }

    with patch(
        "litellm.proxy.agent_endpoints.agent_registry.global_agent_registry"
    ) as registry:
        registry.get_agent_by_id.return_value = agent
        admitted = await asyncio.gather(
            handler.async_pre_call_hook(auth, cache, data, ""),
            handler.async_pre_call_hook(auth, cache, data, ""),
        )

    key = handler._make_cache_key("session-synthetic")

    # Simulate two successful calls costing $0.08 each
    await handler._increment_spend(key, 0.08)
    await handler._increment_spend(key, 0.08)

    print(
        {
            "admitted": admitted,
            "final_spend": await handler._get_current_spend(key),
            "budget": 0.10,
        }
    )


asyncio.run(main())
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
{'admitted': [None, None], 'final_spend': 0.16, 'budget': 0.1}
```

Both requests are admitted while the session has zero recorded spend. Each synthetic request costs less than the $0.10 cap, but together they finish at $0.16

A subsequent request will be rejected, but the session budget has already been exceeded by 60%

### Current-code analysis

The pre-call hook reads current spend and rejects only when the already-recorded value is at least the cap

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/proxy/hooks/max_budget_per_session_limiter.py#L83-L125

The success hook increments spend only after the provider call finishes

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/proxy/hooks/max_budget_per_session_limiter.py#L127-L171

The Redis Lua script performs an atomic `INCRBYFLOAT` with TTL, but it contains no maximum-budget comparison or reservation token tied to admission

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/proxy/hooks/max_budget_per_session_limiter.py#L34-L57

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/proxy/hooks/max_budget_per_session_limiter.py#L230-L269

### Suggested correction

Reserve an estimated maximum request cost during the pre-call hook with one atomic compare-and-increment operation against the session cap

Reconcile the reservation to actual response cost on success, and release it on failure or cancellation. The existing proxy budget-reservation flow may provide a reusable pattern

For Redis, admission needs one Lua operation that checks current plus requested reservation against the cap and increments only when allowed. The in-memory fallback needs equivalent per-session synchronization

Regression coverage should include two simultaneous requests whose individual estimates fit but whose sum exceeds the cap, concurrent requests across two handler instances sharing Redis, success reconciliation, failure release, and TTL behavior

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

Commit `24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c`

title: [Bug]: Image and video completion costs bypass configured discounts and margins
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I searched open and closed issues before filing
- [x] I found no existing issue for image/video early returns bypassing `cost_discount_config` and `cost_margin_config`

### What happened?

`completion_cost` applies provider discounts and margins to the generic completion path and to search, but image-generation and video-generation branches return raw provider cost before reaching either adjustment

As a result, the same provider-level pricing policy behaves differently by modality. Chat costs reflect configured contract discounts or internal billing margins, while image and video costs do not

This affects the returned completion cost and downstream values derived from it, including spend tracking, budget accounting, response-cost headers, and internal chargeback calculations

The reproduction uses synthetic usage and an invalid example URL. It makes no provider or network call

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Check out commit `24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c`
2. Run this script from the repository root

```python
import litellm
from litellm.types.utils import (
    ImageObject,
    ImageResponse,
    ImageUsage,
    ImageUsageInputTokensDetails,
)

usage = ImageUsage(
    input_tokens=100,
    output_tokens=5000,
    total_tokens=5100,
    input_tokens_details=ImageUsageInputTokensDetails(
        text_tokens=100,
        image_tokens=0,
    ),
)
response = ImageResponse(
    created=1,
    data=[ImageObject(url="https://example.invalid/image.png")],
)
response.usage = usage

old_discount = litellm.cost_discount_config
old_margin = litellm.cost_margin_config

try:
    litellm.cost_discount_config = {}
    litellm.cost_margin_config = {}
    raw = litellm.completion_cost(
        completion_response=response,
        model="gpt-image-1",
        custom_llm_provider="openai",
        call_type="image_generation",
    )

    litellm.cost_discount_config = {"openai": 0.10}
    litellm.cost_margin_config = {"openai": 0.20}
    configured = litellm.completion_cost(
        completion_response=response,
        model="gpt-image-1",
        custom_llm_provider="openai",
        call_type="image_generation",
    )

    print(
        {
            "raw": raw,
            "configured": configured,
            "expected_discount_then_margin": raw * 0.90 * 1.20,
        }
    )
finally:
    litellm.cost_discount_config = old_discount
    litellm.cost_margin_config = old_margin
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
{
  'raw': 0.2005,
  'configured': 0.2005,
  'expected_discount_then_margin': 0.21654000000000004
}
```

The configured result should be the raw cost after the 10% provider discount and then the 20% provider margin, matching the order used by the generic completion path

The image branch provides a concrete reproduction. The video branch has the same control-flow defect because both the duration-aware and fallback paths also return before shared post-processing

### Current-code analysis

The image-generation branch directly returns `route_image_generation_cost_calculator`

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/cost_calculator.py#L1334-L1347

Both video-generation paths directly return their raw calculator result

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/cost_calculator.py#L1348-L1392

The search-specific path explicitly applies discount and margin before returning, showing that modality-specific cost paths are expected to honor the configuration

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/cost_calculator.py#L1440-L1485

The generic completion path applies the same two adjustments much later, after image and video have already returned

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/cost_calculator.py#L1598-L1638

The settings UI describes these as provider discounts and margins for internal billing/cost recovery, without a modality exclusion

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/cost_tracking_settings.py

### Suggested correction

Route every billable modality through one shared finalization helper that applies provider discount, provider/global margin, and cost-breakdown storage before returning

Regression coverage should compare configured and unconfigured costs for image generation and both video branches, including provider-specific discounts, provider-specific margins, global margins, fixed margins, and combined percentage/fixed margins

It would also be useful to audit other early returns in `completion_cost` against the same finalization contract

SDK and Proxy cost tracking

title: [Bug]: Built-in tool cost tracking stops after the first detected tool
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I searched open and closed issues before filing
- [x] I found no existing issue for the mutually exclusive control flow in `get_cost_for_built_in_tools`

### What happened?

`StandardBuiltInToolCostTracking.get_cost_for_built_in_tools` returns immediately after the first matching built-in tool category

If a response contains both a web-search call and a file-search call, the web-search fee is returned and file-search cost is never evaluated. If web search is absent but file search is present, the file-search branch returns before Azure assistant feature costs are evaluated

These are independent billable tool categories. The Responses API accepts a list of tools, and OpenAI publishes separate per-call prices for web search and file search

OpenAI tool configuration:

https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools

OpenAI tool pricing:

https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing#tools

The dispatcher therefore models independent fees as an exclusive choice and can understate response cost, spend logs, and budget consumption

The reproduction below uses synthetic handler return values to isolate dispatcher behavior and makes no provider or network call

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Check out commit `24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c`
2. Run this script from the repository root

```python
from unittest.mock import patch

from litellm.litellm_core_utils.llm_cost_calc.tool_call_cost_tracking import (
    StandardBuiltInToolCostTracking as ToolCosts,
)

with patch.object(
    ToolCosts,
    "response_object_includes_web_search_call",
    return_value=True,
), patch.object(
    ToolCosts,
    "response_object_includes_file_search_call",
    return_value=True,
), patch.object(
    ToolCosts,
    "_handle_web_search_cost",
    return_value=1.0,
) as web_cost, patch.object(
    ToolCosts,
    "_handle_file_search_cost",
    return_value=2.0,
) as file_cost:
    actual = ToolCosts.get_cost_for_built_in_tools(
        model="synthetic-model",
        response_object=object(),
        custom_llm_provider="openai",
    )

print(
    {
        "actual": actual,
        "additive_expected": 3.0,
        "web_handler_calls": web_cost.call_count,
        "file_handler_calls": file_cost.call_count,
    }
)
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
{
  'actual': 1.0,
  'additive_expected': 3.0,
  'web_handler_calls': 1,
  'file_handler_calls': 0
}
```

The mocked values are arbitrary synthetic costs. The important result is that the second detected tool handler is never called

### Current-code analysis

The top-level dispatcher returns the web-search result immediately, then returns the file-search result immediately, and only reaches Azure assistant costs when neither earlier branch returns

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/litellm_core_utils/llm_cost_calc/tool_call_cost_tracking.py#L27-L74

The Azure assistant helper already demonstrates the intended additive pattern by summing vector-store, computer-use, and code-interpreter costs into `total_cost`

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/litellm_core_utils/llm_cost_calc/tool_call_cost_tracking.py#L128-L153

### Suggested correction

Initialize a total at zero, evaluate every applicable independent tool category, add each result, and return the total after all handlers run

If any categories are intentionally mutually exclusive for a particular provider or API, encode that restriction explicitly by provider/call type instead of using unconditional early returns

Regression coverage should use a response fixture containing both `web_search_call` and `file_search_call`, then assert that both handlers contribute to the final cost. Azure-specific coverage should also verify that search cost does not suppress configured assistant feature cost when that combination is supported

title: [Bug]: DashScope tiered pricing uses graduated slices instead of the request-size tier
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I searched open and closed issues before filing
- [x] #30738 concerns string coercion inside DashScope tier data and #21249 concerns missing flat prices during budget enforcement, so neither covers this pricing-model mismatch

### What happened?

The DashScope cost calculator applies graduated, income-tax-style slicing to `tiered_pricing`, while Alibaba Model Studio selects one tier from the total input-token count and bills all input and output tokens at that tier's unit prices

The proxy budget reservation code already implements the request-size model through `select_tier_for_input`, so reservation estimates and post-response spend accounting also disagree with each other

This can materially understate logged spend and weaken budget enforcement for large Qwen requests. Cached input is especially inconsistent because the current calculator tiers the cached-token count independently from zero instead of selecting a rate from the request's total input size

Alibaba's current pricing rule is documented here:

https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/model-studio/model-pricing

The relevant rule says the unit price is selected by total input tokens in one request and all tokens in that request use the corresponding tier

All token counts in the reproduction are synthetic and no provider request is made

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Check out commit `24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c`
2. Run this script from the repository root

```python
from litellm.llms.dashscope.cost_calculator import cost_per_token
from litellm.types.utils import Usage
from litellm.utils import get_model_info
from litellm.litellm_core_utils.llm_cost_calc.tiered_pricing import (
    select_tier_for_input,
    tier_rate,
)

model = "qwen-flash"
input_tokens = 300_000
output_tokens = 2_000
usage = Usage(
    prompt_tokens=input_tokens,
    completion_tokens=output_tokens,
    total_tokens=input_tokens + output_tokens,
)

actual_input, actual_output = cost_per_token(model, usage)
model_info = get_model_info(
    model=model,
    custom_llm_provider="dashscope",
)
tier = select_tier_for_input(
    model_info["tiered_pricing"],
    input_tokens,
)
expected_input = input_tokens * tier_rate(tier, "input_cost_per_token")
expected_output = output_tokens * tier_rate(tier, "output_cost_per_token")

print(
    {
        "actual_input": actual_input,
        "actual_output": actual_output,
        "actual_total": actual_input + actual_output,
        "request_tier_input": expected_input,
        "request_tier_output": expected_output,
        "request_tier_total": expected_input + expected_output,
    }
)
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
{
  'actual_input': 0.023799999999999998,
  'actual_output': 0.0007999999999999999,
  'actual_total': 0.024599999999999997,
  'request_tier_input': 0.075,
  'request_tier_output': 0.004,
  'request_tier_total': 0.079
}
```

For the current `qwen-flash` map, the two tiers are:

```python
[
    {
        "range": [0, 256000],
        "input_cost_per_token": 5e-08,
        "output_cost_per_token": 4e-07,
    },
    {
        "range": [256000, 1000000],
        "input_cost_per_token": 2.5e-07,
        "output_cost_per_token": 2e-06,
    },
]
```

A 300,000-input-token request selects the second tier. The current result instead charges the first 256,000 input tokens at the lower rate, the remaining 44,000 at the higher rate, and the 2,000 output tokens at the first tier because completion tokens are tiered independently

### Current-code analysis

DashScope prompt cost calls `calculate_tiered_cost` separately for text input and cached input

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/llms/dashscope/cost_calculator.py#L45-L68

Completion and reasoning tokens are also passed independently to the graduated helper

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/llms/dashscope/cost_calculator.py#L77-L100

The shared helper explicitly implements graduated slicing

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/litellm_core_utils/llm_cost_calc/tiered_pricing.py#L28-L95

The same module separately documents and implements Alibaba's all-or-nothing request-size tier selection

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/litellm_core_utils/llm_cost_calc/tiered_pricing.py#L102-L132

Budget reservation uses the request-size selector for both input-only and maximum-cost estimates

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/proxy/spend_tracking/budget_reservation.py#L988-L1003

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/proxy/spend_tracking/budget_reservation.py#L1044-L1064

### Suggested correction

Select one DashScope tier from total request input tokens before splitting plain, cached, completion, and reasoning tokens

Apply that selected tier's matching rate to every token category, including cache-specific and reasoning-specific rates with the existing fallbacks

Regression coverage should include exact tier boundaries, input beyond the final tier, mixed plain and cached input, and output token counts that would independently fall into a different tier

title: [Bug]: /v1/responses reserves one token and reconciles ResponseAPIUsage as zero
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I searched open and closed issues before filing
- [x] #18671 reports the same external symptom on v1.80.11, but it was closed as stale/not planned and the two current code paths below remain reproducible on commit `24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c`

### What happened?

The proxy TPM limiter undercounts `/v1/responses` in both phases of its reservation/reconciliation flow

Before the provider call, a Responses request with non-empty `input` is classified like an embeddings request, so its output reservation is zero. The estimator also ignores the Responses API field `max_output_tokens`

After a successful provider call, the limiter receives `ResponseAPIUsage`, but `_get_total_tokens_from_usage` only handles the legacy `Usage` object or a `dict` with `prompt_tokens` and `completion_tokens`. A real `ResponseAPIUsage` object therefore reconciles as zero input, zero output, and zero total tokens

This combination can fully refund an already too-small reservation. TPM limits for keys, teams, users, and models can be under-enforced for Responses traffic, especially with concurrent requests

All values and identifiers below are synthetic and the reproduction makes no provider or network call

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Check out commit `24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c`
2. Run this script from the repository root

```python
from litellm.caching.caching import DualCache
from litellm.proxy.utils import InternalUsageCache
from litellm.proxy.hooks.parallel_request_limiter_v3 import (
    _PROXY_MaxParallelRequestsHandler_v3,
)
from litellm.types.llms.openai import ResponseAPIUsage

handler = _PROXY_MaxParallelRequestsHandler_v3(
    InternalUsageCache(DualCache())
)

request = {
    "model": "gpt-4.1",
    "input": "hello",
    "max_output_tokens": 4096,
}
usage = ResponseAPIUsage(
    input_tokens=123,
    output_tokens=456,
    total_tokens=579,
)

print("estimate", handler._estimate_tokens_for_request(request))
print(
    "usage",
    {
        kind: handler._get_total_tokens_from_usage(usage, kind)
        for kind in ("input", "output", "total")
    },
)
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
estimate 1
usage {'input': 0, 'output': 0, 'total': 0}
```

Expected values for this synthetic case are:

```shell
estimate >= 4097
usage {'input': 123, 'output': 456, 'total': 579}
```

The estimate expectation is one approximate input token plus the explicit 4096-token output limit

### Current-code analysis

The request estimator reads `input` with an embeddings comment, only recognizes `max_tokens` and `max_completion_tokens`, then gives any non-empty `input` zero output tokens

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/proxy/hooks/parallel_request_limiter_v3.py#L481-L554

The small-TPM hard-cap path independently uses `data.get("input") is not None` as its embeddings test

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/proxy/hooks/parallel_request_limiter_v3.py#L2487-L2501

The usage reconciler checks `Usage` and `dict`, but not `ResponseAPIUsage`. Its Responses-related `dict` comment is also inconsistent with the fields it reads because it looks for `prompt_tokens` and `completion_tokens`

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/proxy/hooks/parallel_request_limiter_v3.py#L2626-L2678

The actual Responses usage type exposes `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `total_tokens`, and `input_tokens_details.cached_tokens`

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/types/llms/openai.py#L1208-L1236

### Suggested correction

Classify the estimator by call type instead of the presence of `input`, and recognize `max_output_tokens` for Responses requests

Normalize `ResponseAPIUsage` through the existing Responses-to-chat usage transformation, or explicitly support both object and dictionary forms with `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `total_tokens`, and `input_tokens_details.cached_tokens`

Regression coverage should exercise a real `ResponseAPIUsage` instance, all three limiter token modes, cached-input handling, and a Responses request containing `input` plus `max_output_tokens`

Proxy

title: [Docs]: REDIS_URL prod warning is stale; the perf gap it cites is fixed
body:
### What happened?

The caching docs still advise against `REDIS_URL` in production on performance grounds:

> we **don't** recommend using REDIS_URL in prod. We've noticed a performance difference between using it vs. redis_host, port, etc.

That guidance was correct when it was written, and it traces back to #3188. The cause was connection churn: the url path discarded the shared pool and opened roughly two new connections per request, which is ruinous over TLS because each one pays a fresh handshake.

Current code pools correctly, and the gap is gone. Measured against a local redis behind a TCP relay injecting a fixed one-way delay, with redis in the request path on every call (response caching with unique prompts, 500 requests, 50 concurrent workers):

| version | mode | req/s | connections opened |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.35.17 | url | 540 | 1002 |
| 1.35.17 | host/port | 742 | 50 |
| current (1.95.0) | url | 650 | 50 |
| current (1.95.0) | host/port | 690 | 50 |

Over TLS the old churn cost 83.9 req/s against 462.1 on current code, with 1007 connections against 52. On current code url and host/port are within run to run noise of each other, so the stated reason for the recommendation no longer holds. Full detail is in a comment on #3188.

The recommendation should not simply be deleted, because `REDIS_URL` still has a real caveat, just a different one. Only `url`, `timeout` and `max_connections` are forwarded into the pool in `get_redis_connection_pool`, so any setting supplied outside the URL string is silently dropped. A `REDIS_PASSWORD` set alongside a `REDIS_URL` never reaches the client, and the same applies to ssl options and socket timeouts. Everything has to be embedded in the URL itself, as in `redis://user:pass@host:6379/0?socket_timeout=5`.

So the suggested doc change is to drop the performance claim and replace it with the configuration caveat, noting that url-based setups must carry credentials and options inside the URL string.

### Relevant issues

Reason for the original guidance: #3188

title: [Bug]:  RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration in success_handler/failure_handler under concurrent logging
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

The synchronous `Logging.success_handler` and `Logging.failure_handler` (`litellm/litellm_core_utils/litellm_logging.py`) iterate the live `self.model_call_details` dict directly (`for k, v in self.model_call_details.items():`) while building the kwargs passed to sync callbacks (langfuse, logfire, greenscale, athina, traceloop).

These sync handlers run on a **worker thread** (dispatched via `executor.submit` / `threading.Thread`), while `async_success_handler` / `async_failure_handler` run on the **event loop** and insert **new keys** into the *same* `self.model_call_details` object (e.g. `async_complete_streaming_response`, `response_cost`, `standard_logging_object`, and — on failures — `log_event_type`, `exception`, `traceback_exception`, `end_time`). When the async path inserts a key while the sync loop is mid-iteration, Python raises `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`, which aborts that callback's logging for the request (the exception is swallowed by the handler's non-blocking try/except, so the log is silently dropped).

The sync and async handlers are dispatched concurrently, without serialization, on several paths:

- **Success:** the async wrapper enqueues `async_success_handler` on the logging worker (`litellm/utils.py`, `_client_async_logging_helper`) and then immediately `executor.submit(success_handler)` via `handle_sync_success_callbacks_for_async_calls` whenever a sync callback (e.g. `langfuse`, `s3`) is configured — with no `await` between them.
- **Failure:** `litellm/router.py` pairs `asyncio.create_task(async_failure_handler)` with `threading.Thread(target=failure_handler).start()` on the same logging object (multiple sites).

Root cause: iterating a live mutable dict that a concurrent thread/loop can resize. Fix: snapshot the items view with `list(...)` before iterating.

### Steps to Reproduce

Plain concurrent-mutation race — reproduces at unit level, no provider/infra needed. A dict whose key comparison mutates the parent dict stands in for a concurrent async writer inserting a key mid-iteration:

```python
d = {}

class Poison(str):
    def __ne__(self, other):
        if "late" not in d:          # a concurrent async handler inserting a new key
            d["late"] = "x"
        return str.__ne__(self, other)
    def __hash__(self):
        return str.__hash__(self)

d[Poison("original_response")] = 1
d["a"] = 2
d["b"] = 3

# mirrors success_handler's langfuse copy-loop:
kwargs = {}
for k, v in d.items():               # RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration
    if k != "original_response":
        kwargs[k] = v
```

Real-world path: an SDK/proxy request with any sync callback configured (`langfuse`, `s3`, …) under concurrency, so the event-loop `async_success_handler` inserts `standard_logging_object` / `response_cost` while the worker-thread `success_handler` copies `model_call_details` for the sync callback.

### Relevant log output

```shell
RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration
  File ".../litellm/litellm_core_utils/litellm_logging.py", line 2219, in success_handler
    for k, v in self.model_call_details.items():
```

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.94.0-rc.3

title: [Bug]: [Security]: Raw virtual key persisted in cleartext under `user_api_key_hash` in standard logging metadata
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

`StandardLoggingMetadata.user_api_key_hash` is emitted into long-lived logging sinks (e.g. the S3 request/response logs). It is meant to hold a **hash** of the virtual key, never the key itself. But both functions that build the standard logging metadata blind-copy `user_api_key_hash` verbatim from the caller's input metadata, so a **raw** `sk-...` virtual key (or a JWT) placed in that field is persisted in cleartext.

`user_api_key_hash` is a `StandardLoggingMetadata` field (`litellm/types/utils.py`), so it is included in the key set that both builders copy directly from input metadata:

`litellm/litellm_core_utils/litellm_logging.py` — `StandardLoggingPayloadSetup.get_standard_logging_metadata` (~line 4690):

```python
if isinstance(metadata, dict):
    for key in metadata.keys() & _STANDARD_LOGGING_METADATA_KEYS:
        clean_metadata[key] = metadata[key]  # type: ignore   # <-- copies user_api_key_hash verbatim

    user_api_key = metadata.get("user_api_key")
    if user_api_key and isinstance(user_api_key, str) and is_valid_sha256_hash(user_api_key):
        clean_metadata["user_api_key_hash"] = user_api_key
```

`litellm/litellm_core_utils/litellm_logging.py` — module-level `get_standard_logging_metadata` (~line 5532):

```python
if isinstance(metadata, dict):
    for key in StandardLoggingMetadata.__annotations__.keys():
        if key in metadata:
            clean_metadata[key] = metadata[key]  # type: ignore   # <-- same verbatim copy

    if metadata.get("user_api_key") is not None:
        if is_valid_sha256_hash(str(metadata.get("user_api_key"))):
            clean_metadata["user_api_key_hash"] = metadata.get("user_api_key")  # this is the hash
```

Note the only guarding logic present validates the *separate* `user_api_key` field with `is_valid_sha256_hash` before promoting it into `user_api_key_hash`. There is **no such guard on `user_api_key_hash` itself** — it is copied as-is by the loop above.

The proxy auth path normally hashes the key before it reaches logging, but several paths can place a raw value in this field: the `master_key is None` early-return in proxy auth, an SDK caller passing `user_api_key_hash` directly, or a future regression upstream of logging.

**Expected:** whatever is persisted under `user_api_key_hash` is always a hash — a raw `sk-...` key or JWT arriving in that field must be hashed at the logging boundary before it reaches any sink.

**Actual:** a raw `sk-...` key (or JWT) in the input `user_api_key_hash` is copied verbatim into the standard logging payload and written to the configured logging sinks (S3, etc.) in cleartext — a credential-in-cleartext leak in durable storage. The failure is silent (no error, no warning).

**Proposed fix:**

Sanitize the field at the logging boundary in both builders, delegating credential detection + hashing to the existing canonical auth helper `UserAPIKeyAuth._safe_hash_litellm_api_key` (single source of truth — covers `sk-` via `hash_token`, JWT as `hashed-jwt-<h>`, and strips a `Bearer ` prefix), so the stored hash matches what the auth layer produces elsewhere and attribution joins still work. Non-credential / already-hashed / non-string values pass through unchanged.

```python
def _sanitize_user_api_key_hash(value: Optional[Any]) -> Optional[str]:
    """Hash a raw virtual key/JWT so it is never persisted to a log sink in cleartext."""
    if not value or not isinstance(value, str):
        return value
    if is_valid_sha256_hash(value):
        return value
    candidate = value.strip()
    if candidate[:7].lower() == "bearer ":
        candidate = candidate[7:].strip()

    from litellm.proxy._types import UserAPIKeyAuth

    sanitized = UserAPIKeyAuth._safe_hash_litellm_api_key(candidate)
    return sanitized if sanitized != candidat
```

Applied at both builders right after the copy loop:

```python
clean_metadata["user_api_key_hash"] = _saniti_metadata.get("user_api_key_hash"))
```

**Related:**
- `UserAPIKeyAuth._safe_hash_litellm_api_key`py` — the canonical key/JWT hasher this fixreuses (the auth layer already calls it to hash keys before they are logged).
- `is_valid_sha256_hash` in `litellm/litellm_.py` — the existing guard used for the`user_api_key` promotion path; this fix reuses it for the short-circuit.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Reproduces with the `litellm` package alone (no proxy, no cloud, no provider):

```python
from litellm.litellm_core_utils.litellm_logging import (
    StandardLoggingPayloadSetup,
)

# A raw virtual key placed under user_api_key_hash (e.g. via the master_key=None
# early-return, an SDK caller, or a regression upstream of logging).
metadata = {"user_api_key_hash": "sk-1234567890abcdefghijklmnop"}

result = StandardLoggingPayloadSetup.get_standard_logging_metadata(metadata)
print(result["user_api_key_hash"])
```

2. Observe the output:

```
sk-1234567890abcdefghijklmnop
```

The raw `sk-...` key is returned verbatim in the standard logging metadata — and from there is written to the configured logging sinks (S3 request/response logs, etc.) in cleartext.

3. This is the bug: `user_api_key_hash` is documented and named as a hash and lands in durable, long-lived log storage, but a raw credential in that field is persisted unhashed. Same result for the module-level `get_standard_logging_metadata` and for a `Bearer sk-...` / whitespace-padded / raw-JWT value.

### Relevant log output

```shell

```

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.94.0-rc.3

title: [Bug]: Hanging-request Slack alert always shows empty Key Alias / Team Alias (metadata read from wrong location at pre-call time)
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

When the `llm_requests_hanging` Slack alert fires, the **Key Alias** and **Team Alias** fields are always blank, regardless of which key/team made the request. This makes the alert unable to identify who is responsible for the hang.

**Expected:** the alert shows the key/team alias of the hanging request.
**Actual:** `Key Alias` and `Team Alias` are always empty.

**Root cause (on `litellm_internal_staging`):**

`AlertingHangingRequestCheck.add_request_to_hanging_request_check` reads request metadata via `get_litellm_metadata_from_kwargs()`:

- `litellm/integrations/SlackAlerting/hanging_request_check.py:60`

  ```python
  request_metadata = get_litellm_metadata_from_kwargs(kwargs=request_data)
  ```

- `litellm/integrations/SlackAlerting/hanging_request_check.py:74-75`

  ```python
  key_alias=request_metadata.get("user_api_key_alias", ""),
  team_alias=request_metadata.get("user_api_key_team_alias", ""),
  ```

- `litellm/litellm_core_utils/core_helpers.py:169` — `get_litellm_metadata_from_kwargs` reads **only** `kwargs["litellm_params"]["metadata"]` / `["litellm_metadata"]` and returns `{}` when there is no `litellm_params` key.

The hanging check is scheduled from the proxy **pre-call** path (`_init_response_taking_too_long_task(data=data)` → `response_taking_too_long(request_data=data)` → `add_request_to_hanging_request_check(request_data=data)`). At pre-call time the request dict carries the alias at top-level `data["metadata"]["user_api_key_alias"]`, but there is **no top-level `data["litellm_params"]` key yet** — that is populated later inside the SDK completion call. So `get_litellm_metadata_from_kwargs` returns `{}` and both aliases resolve to `""` for every proxy request.

(The sibling post-call callback `response_taking_too_long_callback` reads `kwargs["litellm_params"]["metadata"]` and works, because that path runs after `litellm_params` is constructed — confirming the two paths genuinely differ in where the metadata lives.)

### Steps to Reproduce

1. `config.yaml`:

   ```yaml
   model_list:
     - model_name: hang-test
       litellm_params:
         model: openai/gpt-4o
         api_base: http://127.0.0.1:9999/v1   # a socket that accepts but never responds
         api_key: sk-fake

   general_settings:
     alerting: ["slack"]
     alert_types: ["llm_requests_hanging"]
     alerting_threshold: 1   # seconds; keep low so the alert fires fast

   environment_variables:
     SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL: "https://hooks.slack.com/services/XXX/YYY/ZZZ"
   ```

2. Start a listener that accepts the connection but never replies, so the request hangs past the threshold:

   ```bash
   # never sends a response body -> request hangs
   while true; do printf '' | nc -l 9999; done
   ```

3. Start the proxy:

   ```bash
   litellm --config config.yaml
   ```

4. Create a key with an alias:

   ```bash
   curl -s http://localhost:4000/key/generate \
   ```

title: [Bug]: [Security] print_verbose prints api_key and raw control chars to stdout when set_verbose=True (stdout path not redacted or sanitized)
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

Every `print_verbose` helper in the codebase prints its argument **raw** to stdout when `litellm.set_verbose is True`. Callers routinely pass dict-shaped diagnostic payloads (e.g. `model_call_details`) that contain `api_key` (and, on the proxy, master/virtual keys, and provider Bearer tokens), so the full secret is emitted verbatim to stdout and captured by container/pod log collectors. In addition, model- and request-controlled content reaches these same stdout paths (e.g. the async streaming line logger), so unescaped CR/LF/Unicode-separator/control characters allow log forging and terminal-escape injection (CWE-117).

The `verbose_logger` path is already redacted by `SecretRedactionFilter`; only the `set_verbose` stdout `print(...)` branch is unprotected. There are **multiple** copies of `print_verbose` across the code, and they share this same unredacted-stdout pattern:

- `litellm/utils.py::print_verbose`
- `litellm/_logging.py::print_verbose`
- `litellm/main.py::print_verbose` (prints provider streaming chunks — `line in async streaming`)
- `litellm/caching/caching.py::print_verbose`
- `litellm/litellm_core_utils/streaming_handler.py::print_verbose`
- `litellm/proxy/utils.py::print_verbose` (redacts, but does not sanitize control chars)
- `litellm/proxy/guardrails/guardrail_hooks/presidio.py::_OPTIONAL_PresidioPIIMasking.print_verbose`
- `litellm/proxy/hooks/batch_redis_get.py::_PROXY_BatchRedisRequests.print_verbose`
- `litellm/proxy/hooks/prompt_injection_detection.py::_OPTIONAL_PromptInjectionDetection.print_verbose`
- `litellm/proxy/hooks/parallel_request_limiter.py::_PROXY_MaxParallelRequestsHandler.print_verbose`

Representative offending snippet (`litellm/utils.py`):

```python
def print_verbose(print_statement, logger_only=False, log_level="DEBUG"):
    try:
        if log_level == "DEBUG":
            verbose_logger.debug(print_statement)   # redacted by SecretRedactionFilter
        ...
        if litellm.set_verbose is True and logger_only is False:
            print(print_statement)  # noqa: T201    # <-- RAW: not redacted, not sanitized
    except Exception:
        pass
```

**Expected:** the stdout path masks secrets (matching what `litellm/_logging.py`'s stdout write already does with `redact_secrets(...)`) and neutralizes control characters that could forge log lines or inject terminal escapes. Redaction should still honor the `LITELLM_DISABLE_REDACT_SECRETS=true` opt-out.

**Actual:** the `api_key` value reaches stdout unredacted (exposing credentials to any log sink that captures stdout), and CR/LF/Unicode-separator/C0/C1/DEL characters pass through unescaped (log-injection / terminal-manipulation vector). No error is raised — the exposure is silent.

**Proposed fix:** redact then sanitize before every `set_verbose` stdout print, e.g. a single shared helper:

```python
# litellm/_logging.py
def _sanitize_log_message(message: str) -> str:
    for ch, esc in {
        "\r": "\\r", "\n": "\\n", "\x85": "\\x85",
        " ": "\\u2028", " ": "\\u2029",
    }.items():
        message = message.replace(ch, esc)
    return re.sub(r"[\x00-\x08\x0b\x0c\x0e-\x1f\x7f-\x9f]", "?", message)

def _redact_and_sanitize(value) -> str:
    return _sanitize_log_message(redact_secrets(str(value)))
```

and route each `print_verbose` stdout branch through `print(_redact_and_sanitize(print_statement))`. `redact_secrets` already exists in `litellm/_logging.py` and is a no-op when `LITELLM_DISABLE_REDACT_SECRETS=true`; the sanitizer is independent of the opt-out.

**Related:**
- #24813 (merged) — added `SecretRedactionFilter` / the redaction infrastructure this fix reuses.
- The separate "`print_verbose` doesn't emit through `verbose_logger` when `set_verbose` is False" behavior (#32318 / PRs #32495, #32326) is deliberately **out of scope** for this security fix.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Install current `main` / latest release (`pip install litellm`).
2. Run (no proxy, cloud, or provider credentials required):

```python
import litellm
from litellm.utils import print_verbose

litellm.set_verbose = True
print_verbose({
    "model": "gpt-4o",
    "api_key": "sk-secret-DO-NOT-LEAK-1234567890abcdef",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}],
})
print_verbose("attacker\r\nFORGED-LOG-LINE injected")
```

3. Observe stdout:

```
{'model': 'gpt-4o', 'api_key': 'sk-secret-DO-NOT-LEAK-1234567890abcdef', 'messages': [{'role': 'user', 'content': 'hi'}]}
attacker
FORGED-LOG-LINE injected
```

The `api_key` is printed verbatim, and the CR/LF splits the second call into a forged extra log line. The same happens organically on real calls (many paths pass `model_call_details`, which carries `api_key`, through `print_verbose` when `set_verbose=True`), including the `litellm.main.print_verbose` path that logs provider streaming chunks.

### Relevant log output

```shell

```

title: [Feature]: Prometheus exporter cannot attribute spend, latency or traffic to a region or call type
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### Context

Filing this at Krrish's request after a Discord thread. We run LiteLLM Proxy in production in front of Azure OpenAI deployments spread across several regions plus Bedrock, and we maintain a patched build of `litellm/integrations/prometheus.py` because the shipped exporter cannot answer the questions we need it to answer. This issue documents what we hit, what we changed, and which of those changes I think belong upstream. Happy to send each as a separate PR.

All line references are against `litellm_internal_staging` at `24123269ccb7`, since that is the default branch and where PRs land. The same lines are present on `main`.

cc @yucheng-berri, who owns most of the recent work in this file.

---

### Problem 1: rate-limit gauges silently drop a value of `0`

`set_llm_deployment_success_metrics` guards both gauges with a truthy check:

```python
# litellm/integrations/prometheus.py:2694
if remaining_requests:
    ...
    self.litellm_remaining_requests_metric.labels(**_labels).set(remaining_requests)

# litellm/integrations/prometheus.py:2708
if remaining_tokens:
    ...
    self.litellm_remaining_tokens_metric.labels(**_labels).set(remaining_tokens)
```

When a provider reports `0` remaining, meaning the quota is actually exhausted, Python reads it as falsy and the gauge is never updated. Prometheus keeps serving the last non-zero value, so an alert on `litellm_remaining_requests_metric == 0` never fires and a dashboard shows healthy headroom during an outage. `0` and "the provider sent no header" both end up indistinguishable.

The same file already handles this correctly elsewhere for the same two variables:

- `_async_set_router_remaining_metrics`, lines 2609 and 2617: `if not already_have_tokens and remaining_tokens is not None:`
- `litellm_remaining_api_key_requests_for_model`, lines 1843 to 1855: `if remaining_requests is None: remaining_requests = sys.maxsize`

So this is an internal inconsistency rather than a design choice.

Filed as #29214. It is now rebased onto `litellm_internal_staging`, retargeted off `main`, conflict-free, and carries a live before and after: with the fix the gauge reads `0`, without it the gauge keeps serving the previous request's `1` while the quota is gone.

---

### Problem 2: there is no region dimension anywhere in the exporter

`region` appears zero times in `litellm/integrations/prometheus.py` and zero times in `litellm/types/integrations/prometheus.py`.

For a single-region install that is fine. For anyone running the same logical model across multiple regions, every region collapses into one time series and the following questions have no answer today:

- Which region is being throttled? `litellm_remaining_requests_metric` carries `api_base`, so the raw URL is technically there, but it is a high-cardinality opaque string rather than a dimension you can group or alert on.
- What are we spending per region? `litellm_spend_metric` has no `api_base` at all.
- Is one region slower? `litellm_llm_api_latency_metric` and `litellm_llm_api_time_to_first_token_metric` have no `api_base` either.

That last point is the crux. `api_base` is present on 10 metrics, all deployment-level, and absent from 29 others including `litellm_spend_metric`, `litellm_requests_metric`, `litellm_total_tokens_metric`, `litellm_request_total_latency_metric` and `litellm_llm_api_latency_metric`. So "derive the region from `api_base`" is not available on the metrics where regional attribution actually matters.

**What we run:** a `region` label resolved in priority order from `litellm_params.region_name`, `litellm_params.aws_region_name`, `litellm_params.vertex_location`, then metadata equivalents. Those are explicit and authoritative. We additionally fall back to parsing the region out of `api_base`, which works well for us but is a heuristic, and I would keep it out of a first PR or put it behind its own flag.

---

### Problem 3: no `call_type` dimension

`call_type` also appears zero times in both files. Chat completions, embeddings, image generation and audio all land in the same `litellm_requests_metric` and `litellm_spend_metric` series. Embedding traffic is typically orders of magnitude higher volume and orders of magnitude lower cost than chat, so mixing them makes both the request-rate and the spend series hard to reason about.

`standard_logging_payload` already carries `call_type`, so this is label plumbing rather than new data collection.

---

### Problem 4 (question, not a claim): `litellm_images_generated_metric` coverage

`_increment_media_generation_metrics` (line 1487) sources the counter from `standard_logging_payload["metadata"]["usage_object"]["output_image_count"]`, and skips when the value is absent.

I have not verified upstream's behaviour against every image provider, so I am asking rather than reporting: is `output_image_count` expected to be populated for all image-generation paths, including Azure DALL-E and Bedrock image models? If some providers do not report it, the counter silently stays at zero for them and a fallback (for example the length of the returned image list on image call types) would help. I am glad to test and send a PR if this is a real gap.

---

### Proposed shape

Problems 2 and 3 are the same shape as #32126, which added `api_provider` to the token, latency, request and cache metrics because those were emitted from call sites that already had the value and there was no way to break the numbers down by provider without it. `region` and `call_type` are the next two dimensions in that list, and both are already available at the same call sites. I would follow that PR directly: add the labels to the default sets, one PR per label, with tests and before/after dashboards.

If you would rather not grow the default label sets, the file also has the opt-in pattern, `litellm.prometheus_emit_stream_label` and `litellm.prometheus_emit_rate_limit_labels`, the latter carrying the comment "Off by default so the metric's historical label set is preserved across upgrade". #30532 is an open request for more label control, so I understand if cardinality is a concern here. Either shape works for us. Tell me which you prefer and I will build it that way.

Suggested split, each one independent:

1. #29214, rebased and ready for review. The `0` fix, two lines plus a regression test.
2. `region` label, resolved only from explicit config fields.
3. `call_type` label.
4. Region inference from `api_base` for AWS and Azure, if you want it. This one is a heuristic, so I would keep it behind a flag regardless of what we decide for 2 and 3.
5. Image counter fallback, if Problem 4 turns out to be real.

---

### Changes we run that I am not proposing upstream

Including these for completeness since the offer was to share what we run in production. I do not think they belong in LiteLLM as-is, and here is why.

- **Pre-computed RPM and TPM gauges** from an in-process sliding window. `rate()` over the existing counters gives the same answer, our implementation sweeps every window under a lock on every request, and it produces wrong numbers under `PROMETHEUS_MULTIPROC_DIR` because each worker only sees its own share of traffic.
- **Moving the `litellm_proxy_total_requests_metric` increment into `async_log_success_event`.** This gives us fully-labelled counts, but it drops requests that never reach an LLM such as auth rejections and non-LLM routes, which changes what the metric means.
- **A reduced `LATENCY_BUCKETS` set**, 15 buckets instead of 35. It roughly halves histogram cardinality and I would happily discuss it separately, but changing bucket boundaries changes every existing `histogram_quantile()` result, so it is not something to slip into another PR.

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

title: [Bug]: `ollama_chat` → Anthropic `/v1/messages` streaming sets `stop_reason: "end_turn"` (not `"tool_use"`) and emits a spurious empty leading text block when the turn contains a tool call
body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

When an `ollama_chat` model is served through the Anthropic `/v1/messages` adapter with `stream: true`, and the model returns a tool call, the streamed response is malformed in two ways:

1. The final `message_delta` carries `stop_reason: "end_turn"` even though the message contains a `tool_use` block. Per the Anthropic Messages spec it MUST be `stop_reason: "tool_use"`.
2. A spurious empty leading text block is emitted first — `content_block` index 0 is `{"type": "text", "text": ""}` (immediately followed by `content_block_stop`) — before the real content.

The `tool_use` block itself and its `input_json_delta` arrive correctly, so the data is on the wire; only the framing (`stop_reason` + the empty text block) is wrong.

**The identical request with `stream: false` is correct** — it returns `stop_reason: "tool_use"` with the full tool input. So this is specific to the streaming translation path.

### Why it matters

Anthropic-Messages tool-runners (Claude Code, the Anthropic SDK's `messages.stream`, and other `/v1/messages` clients) key off `stop_reason == "tool_use"` to decide whether to execute the emitted `tool_use` block. With `stop_reason: "end_turn"` they treat the turn as final assistant text and silently drop the tool call. Combined with the empty leading text block, a client that validates visible payload sees an "empty" turn. In our downstream (OpenClaw gateway) every local-model tool call fails closed — `payloads=0, tools=0`, "agent couldn't generate a response" — so local models via LiteLLM can never call a tool through the Anthropic transport.

### Expected output

- The final `message_delta` should carry `stop_reason: "tool_use"` whenever the streamed message contains at least one `tool_use` content block (matching the non-streaming response and the Anthropic spec).
- No empty leading `{"type": "text", "text": ""}` content block should be emitted (cf. #22930 on sanitizing empty text blocks).

### Steps to Reproduce

### Environment

- **LiteLLM:** v1.93.0 (`ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-database:v1.93.0`)
- **Provider:** `ollama_chat`
- **Endpoint:** `/v1/messages` (Anthropic Messages adapter), `stream: true`
- Reproduces deterministically across scale — from a **1-tool / ~284-input-token** request up to **40 tools / ~27,900 input tokens**. Independent of model reasoning (reproduces with thinking off), tool count, system-prompt size, and JSON-schema complexity. The only variable that flips it is `stream: true` vs `false`.

### Minimal reproduction

**1. `config.yaml`** (any tool-capable Ollama model):

```yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: qwen3
    litellm_params:
      model: ollama_chat/qwen3:8b
      api_base: http://localhost:11434
```

**2. Start the proxy:**

```bash
litellm --config config.yaml   # serves on :4000
```

**3. Streaming — BROKEN.** `/v1/messages` with `stream: true` and one tool:

```bash
curl -sN http://localhost:4000/v1/messages \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -H 'x-api-key: sk-1234' \
  -H 'anthropic-version: 2023-06-01' \
  -d '{
    "model": "qwen3",
    "max_tokens": 512,
    "stream": true,
    "messages": [
      {"role": "user", "content": "What is the weather in San Francisco? Use the get_weather tool."}
    ],
    "tools": [{
      "name": "get_weather",
      "description": "Get the current weather for a city",
      "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}},
        "required": ["city"]
      }
    }]
  }'
```

**4. Non-streaming — CORRECT.** Same request, `"stream": false` — returns `stop_reason: "tool_use"` with the full tool input.



### Relevant log output

```shell
event: content_block_start
data: {"type": "content_block_start", "index": 0, "content_block": {"type": "text", "text": ""}}   <-- spurious empty text block

event: content_block_stop
data: {"type": "content_block_stop", "index": 0}

event: content_block_start
data: {"type": "content_block_start", "index": 2, "content_block": {"type": "tool_use", "id": "...", "name": "read", "input": {}}}

event: content_block_delta
data: {"type": "content_block_delta", "index": 2, "delta": {"type": "input_json_delta", "partial_json": "{\"path\": \"/tmp/ab/report.txt\"}"}}   <-- tool call is correct

event: content_block_stop
data: {"type": "content_block_stop", "index": 2}

event: message_delta
data: {"type": "message_delta", "delta": {"stop_reason": "end_turn"}, ...}   <-- WRONG: tool_use block present, must be "tool_use"

event: message_stop
data: {"type": "message_stop"}
```

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.93.0

_No response_
author: leftathome

title: tool_calls entries with unrecognized shapes are silently dropped instead of raising
body:
When a message in `messages` carries `tool_calls` whose entries don't match the OpenAI nested shape (e.g. `{id, function: "name", arguments: {...}}` — `function` as a string rather than `{name, arguments}`), litellm silently ignores those entries when converting to provider formats (observed with Anthropic: the tool_use block never reaches the API).

The paired `role: "tool"` results DO convert, so the provider rejects the request with an orphaned-tool_result error far from the actual cause:

```
anthropic invalid_request_error: unexpected tool_use_id found in tool_result blocks
```

Repro sketch:

```python
litellm.completion(
    model="anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6",
    messages=[
        {"role": "assistant", "content": "",
         "tool_calls": [{"id": "call_1", "function": "ls", "arguments": {}}]},  # flat shape
        {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "call_1", "content": "..."},
    ],
)
```

Expected: a validation error naming the malformed entry at conversion time. Silent drops of caller data are the hardest failure mode to debug — a loud shape check would have turned a multi-hour investigation into a one-line fix.
